**CURRENT BASELINE — CREATOR WORDING**

> noxivitres are basically a open cyber-organic species built around blackglass, which is basically this living mutagenic material in their body that can rewrite how they’re built instead of just repairing them, so body parts can split, duplicate, detach, regrow, or just completely change depending on the person. they still use nanites and have digital/cybernetic parts, but their body is basically never completely fixed and blackglass can keep changing them over time, which is kinda the whole point of the species. there’s 6 rarities, common, uncommon, rare, legendary, mythic, and unobtanium, with mythic being the really extreme tier kinda like rare protogens and unobtanium being completely creator locked unless i specifically let someone make one.

This NOXIVITRES bible expands that baseline without replacing it. The baseline is the short public explanation; everything after it is material you can keep, rewrite, ignore, or hand to friends to build on.

**NON-NEGOTIABLES FOR VERSION 0.1**

- Noxivitres are cyber-organic and BlackGlass is central to their biology.

- Nanites stay. They are a functional body system, not just a visual effect.

- Anatomy can be rewritten over time; splitting, duplicating, detaching, regrowing, and restructuring body parts are all valid species mechanics.

- There are exactly six rarity labels: Common, Uncommon, Rare, Legendary, Mythic, and Unobtanium.

- Common through Mythic are open. Mythic is the highest extreme open tier.

- Unobtanium is creator locked and only available when the creator specifically allows it.

- Rarity does not automatically equal power, importance, intelligence, morality, or social status.

- Noxivitres should not depend on a standard Protogen silhouette to be recognizable.

- New lore should create more options, not quietly remove options people were already allowed to use.

- Characters still need personalities, relationships, goals, flaws, and lives beyond their rarity and mutation list.

- Riven Solace and Blade are Generation Zero: the first two Noxivitres and the historical reference point for every later origin model.

- Riven Solace and Blade are both Unobtanium Noxivitres. Their Unobtanium classification comes from mature Generation-Zero core architecture and founder-only BlackGlass behavior, not simply from being the first or from having six arms.

- Riven Solace is owned by @n4k2 on Discord. Blade is owned by @altblade on Discord. Species openness never transfers ownership of either character.

Everything else in this document is expandable canon.

**THE FIRST NOXIVITRES — RIVEN & BLADE**

The Difference Between Trait and Mutation helps define identity, boundaries, and the rules that keep the species recognizable without making every character identical. It is part of the baseline rather than a hard ceiling, so later lore can add detail without needing to throw out the whole species concept.

Common should cover the most stable and straightforward expressions; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare supports major structural deviations; Legendary is for designs where several major systems interact; Mythic is the extreme open tier and is intentionally allowed to get ridiculous. Unobtanium is different in kind rather than simply bigger: it is creator-locked because it carries special canon authority, origin-level exceptions, or personally reserved concepts. A public character never needs Unobtanium just to have a visually extreme body. For weaponization limits, classification should therefore look at the whole character: how much structure changed, how many systems have to cooperate, whether the feature is stable, and how much active BlackGlass is required to maintain it. One dramatic-looking detail can still be Common or Uncommon if it is mechanically simple, while a visually subtle trait can push higher if it fundamentally rewrites the body map.

In everyday life, weaponization limits matters through charging or feeding routines, maintenance, device interaction, privacy, repairs, sensory filtering, and the tiny automatic corrections the swarm performs constantly. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note response speed, visible particle behavior, heat, power use, repair quality, and whether a system can keep working when part of the body is physically separated. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of weaponization limits so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Decide whether the feature changes rarity by itself or only when combined with other major traits.

- Write one example of the trait on a calm character and one on a stressed character.

- Design a Common interpretation and a Mythic interpretation of the same idea.

**PART IV — NANITES & CYBERNETICS • ENTRY 098 · [ATLAS](#nox_atlas) / [PART INDEX](#part-iv-quick-index)**
<a id="entry-098"></a>

# **Nanite Exhaustion**

Nanite Exhaustion sits on the nanite/cybernetic side of the species. It exists to make the body function, communicate, repair itself, or control structures that ordinary nerves and muscles could not handle alone.

- Design around what maintenance the nanites perform.

- Decide how it changes balance and movement.

- Account for what emotional states make it more noticeable.

- Extra anatomy needs room to move. Limb sockets, wings, tails, and floating pieces should be placed with actual posture and collision in mind.

- BlackGlass can be weird without being random. Repeated motifs, copied anatomy, and consistent nanite behavior make extreme designs feel intentional.

In practice, this can show up through details like subtle glitching around active mutations, ear or horn structures that integrate with the skull rather than looking glued on, or visible BlackGlass seams. None of those are mandatory; they are examples of how the same rule can produce different silhouettes while still reading as part of one species.

In-world, **Nanite Exhaustion** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: privacy, movement, maintenance, and sleep can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **Nanite Exhaustion**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

A useful way to understand nanite exhaustion is to separate what the character sees from what BlackGlass and the nanites are actually doing underneath. It connects to nanite command hierarchy, swarm behavior, repair logic, signal routing, and cybernetic integration. The working substrate is personal Vitrite strains, local swarm clusters, Glassheart instructions, stored body-map data, and power reserves. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands nanite exhaustion, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for nanite exhaustion is swarm exhaustion, command conflicts, corrupted templates, poor bandwidth, bad calibration, or too many simultaneous repair and mutation tasks. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for nanite exhaustion before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Nanite Exhaustion** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Nanite Exhaustion** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as visible nanite traffic under load and a more compact resting state should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For nanite exhaustion, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Nanite Exhaustion**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Nanite Exhaustion** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, nanite exhaustion matters through charging or feeding routines, maintenance, device interaction, privacy, repairs, sensory filtering, and the tiny automatic corrections the swarm performs constantly. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note response speed, visible particle behavior, heat, power use, repair quality, and whether a system can keep working when part of the body is physically separated. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of nanite exhaustion so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Define what a medical scanner would call this feature.

- Design a Common interpretation and a Mythic interpretation of the same idea.

- Give the trait one practical downside that is not just 'it hurts.'

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
The best way to understand **Nanite Exhaustion** is to imagine the character dealing with it on a boring Tuesday, not only during a transformation scene.

The useful questions here are **local swarm authority, bandwidth, reservoir access, signal routing, heat, and what the Vitrites are allowed to change without asking the Glassheart**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **Nanite Exhaustion**, practical details can include sleep, maintenance, clothing, and movement. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **Nanite Exhaustion** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include temporary fallback behavior, slower response, and extra heat or energy use. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **Nanite Exhaustion** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include subtle BlackGlass seams, a more compact resting state, and visible nanite traffic under load. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through clothing, ordinary social interaction, and movement—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **Nanite Exhaustion**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. Local function can survive degraded network contact, but precision and repair speed usually drop before basic survival does. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- What misconception about **Nanite Exhaustion** would the character be tired of correcting?
- What would a Noxivitre medic see about **Nanite Exhaustion** that an ordinary observer would miss?
- Which parts of **Nanite Exhaustion** are automatic, and which can be deliberately controlled?
- What is the first small sign that **Nanite Exhaustion** is overloaded, damaged, or badly calibrated?

#### Character-facing note

**Nanite Exhaustion** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.


**PART IV — NANITES & CYBERNETICS • ENTRY 099 · [ATLAS](#nox_atlas) / [PART INDEX](#part-iv-quick-index)**

# **Nanite Corruption**

Nanite Corruption sits on the nanite/cybernetic side of the species. It exists to make the body function, communicate, repair itself, or control structures that ordinary nerves and muscles could not handle alone.

- Design around whether the trait is hidden, visible, or selectively revealed.

- Decide whether the trait can be voluntarily suppressed.

- Account for how medical scans classify it.

- If a trait is copied from another species concept, change its construction and reason for existing so it fits BlackGlass biology.

- The open tiers should stay genuinely open. Do not quietly move popular traits into Unobtanium just to make them exclusive later.

In practice, this can show up through details like temporary nanite scaffolding, fractured or floating face plates, or distinctive paw or hand construction. None of those are mandatory; they are examples of how the same rule can produce different silhouettes while still reading as part of one species.

In-world, **Nanite Corruption** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: clothing, sleep, privacy, and maintenance can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **Nanite Corruption**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

For Noxivitres, nanite corruption is treated as a real system rather than a decorative trait. It connects to nanite command hierarchy, swarm behavior, repair logic, signal routing, and cybernetic integration. The working substrate is personal Vitrite strains, local swarm clusters, Glassheart instructions, stored body-map data, and power reserves. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands nanite corruption, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for nanite corruption is swarm exhaustion, command conflicts, corrupted templates, poor bandwidth, bad calibration, or too many simultaneous repair and mutation tasks. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for nanite corruption before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Nanite Corruption** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Nanite Corruption** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as a more compact resting state and visible nanite traffic under load should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For nanite corruption, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Nanite Corruption**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Nanite Corruption** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, nanite corruption matters through charging or feeding routines, maintenance, device interaction, privacy, repairs, sensory filtering, and the tiny automatic corrections the swarm performs constantly. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception.

BlackGlass does not build **Four-Arm Builds** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Four-Arm Builds** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as different arm pairs settling at different resting heights and plates shifting to give the lower shoulders room should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For four-arm builds, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Four-Arm Builds**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Four-Arm Builds** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, four-arm builds matters through doors, chairs, beds, vehicles, hugs, carrying objects, sports, workspaces, and learning where every new body part is without staring at it. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note stance, gait, reach, turning radius, resting position, clothing cuts, furniture fit, and how the form looks when actually moving instead of posing. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of four-arm builds so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Decide whether the feature changes rarity by itself or only when combined with other major traits.

- Design a Common interpretation and a Mythic interpretation of the same idea.

- Give the trait one practical downside that is not just 'it hurts.'

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
A good version of **Four-Arm Builds** feels specific to the person wearing it. The system can be technically complicated without making the character talk like a manual.

The useful questions here are **load paths, range of motion, proprioception, attachment or suspension logic, and the way nearby structures make room for it**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **Four-Arm Builds**, practical details can include sleeping without trapping a lower arm pair, deciding which hands carry weight, shoulder clearance, and sleeve and jacket construction. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **Four-Arm Builds** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include a copied limb defaulting to a neutral guarded pose, crossed proprioception between two hands, and lag in duplicated shoulder control. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **Four-Arm Builds** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include subtle nanite glow around duplicated sockets, plates shifting to give the lower shoulders room, and different arm pairs settling at different resting heights. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through reaching across the torso without self-collision, deciding which hands carry weight, and sleeping without trapping a lower arm pair—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **Four-Arm Builds**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. The safest fallback is usually a mechanically conservative posture or reduced range, not the anatomy vanishing for no reason. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- Which parts of **Four-Arm Builds** are automatic, and which can be deliberately controlled?
- What is the first small sign that **Four-Arm Builds** is overloaded, damaged, or badly calibrated?
- What misconception about **Four-Arm Builds** would the character be tired of correcting?
- What does **Four-Arm Builds** feel like when nothing is wrong?

#### Character-facing note

**Four-Arm Builds** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.

# **Six-Arm Builds**

Six-arm Noxivitres have three complete arm pairs and are one of the oldest stable extreme body plans in the species because both Generation Zero founders, Riven and Blade, eventually developed this configuration. The standard founder pattern is an original upper pair followed by two duplicated pairs, but later Noxivitres can use different spacing or socket geometry as long as the shoulders, torso, nerves, and body map can actually support the arrangement.

- Design around how it changes balance and movement.

- Decide how medical scans classify it.

- Account for what maintenance the nanites perform.

- A cool visual does not automatically need a higher rarity; rarity should track structural complexity, not color or fashion.

- Mutations should still obey the individual's body map unless the story explicitly establishes corruption or instability.

In practice, this can show up through details like adaptive armor that changes with posture, moving surface patterns that react to emotion, or tails with visible mutation history. None of those are mandatory; they are examples of how the same rule can produce different silhouettes while still reading as part of one species.

In-world, **Six-Arm Builds** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: reaching across the torso without self-collision, deciding which hands carry weight, shoulder clearance, and sleeve and jacket construction can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **Six-Arm Builds**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

The important thing about six-arm builds is that it has to work inside a mutable Noxivitre body, not only look good in a reference sheet. It connects to body geometry, socket placement, balance, collision clearance, coordination, and BlackGlass-supported structural variation. The working substrate is the body map, skeletal or synthetic anchors, nerves, actuators, nanite bridges, and adaptive tissue around the changed body plan. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands six-arm builds, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for six-arm builds is a cool-looking design that has no room to move, duplicated structures that collide with each other, poor center of mass, or too many systems competing for the same space. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for six-arm builds before defining flashy secondary effects.

# **Floating Arms**

Floating Arms is a morphology option rather than a mandatory species trait. It should still look BlackGlass-built: the joints, attachment points, floating gaps, plating, and mutation seams should make the feature feel native to the species instead of pasted on.

- Design around how the individual learned to coordinate it.

- Decide whether the trait can be voluntarily suppressed.

- Account for what emotional states make it more noticeable.

- Damage and mutation are different states. A missing part is not automatically a new trait, and a new trait is not automatically an injury.

- Mutations should still obey the individual's body map unless the story explicitly establishes corruption or instability.

In practice, this can show up through details like nonuniform crystalline surfaces, adaptive armor that changes with posture, or glowing nanite channels. None of those are mandatory; they are examples of how the same rule can produce different silhouettes while still reading as part of one species.

In-world, **Floating Arms** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: knowing where a detached part is without looking, shoulder clearance, moving through narrow doors, and charging or maintaining a separated segment can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **Floating Arms**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

In canon, floating arms sits inside the same body-map logic as every other Noxivitre feature. It connects to body geometry, socket placement, balance, collision clearance, coordination, and BlackGlass-supported structural variation. The working substrate is the body map, skeletal or synthetic anchors, nerves, actuators, nanite bridges, and adaptive tissue around the changed body plan. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands floating arms, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for floating arms is a cool-looking design that has no room to move, duplicated structures that collide with each other, poor center of mass, or too many systems competing for the same space. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for floating arms before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Floating Arms** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Floating Arms** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as subtle nanite glow around duplicated sockets and small correction pulses between body and segment should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For floating arms, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Floating Arms**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Floating Arms** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

A practical reference sheet can note stance, gait, reach, turning radius, resting position, clothing cuts, furniture fit, and how the form looks when actually moving instead of posing. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of floating arms so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Define what a medical scanner would call this feature.

- Give the feature a visual tell that becomes obvious during a Glassshift.

- Give the trait one practical downside that is not just 'it hurts.'

- What misconception about **Floating Tails** would the character be tired of correcting?
- How does **Floating Tails** affect clothing, furniture, sleep, travel, or personal space?

#### Character-facing note

**Floating Tails** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. # **Multiple Tails**

Multiple Tails is a morphology option rather than a mandatory species trait. It should still look BlackGlass-built: the joints, attachment points, floating gaps, plating, and mutation seams should make the feature feel native to the species instead of pasted on.

- Design around what social assumptions are attached to it.

- Decide how another species might misunderstand it.

- Account for what maintenance the nanites perform.

- BlackGlass can be weird without being random. Repeated motifs, copied anatomy, and consistent nanite behavior make extreme designs feel intentional.

- Extra anatomy needs room to move. Limb sockets, wings, tails, and floating pieces should be placed with actual posture and collision in mind.

In practice, this can show up through details like asymmetrical glass growths, body segments held together by a nanite bridge, or nonuniform crystalline surfaces. None of those are mandatory; they are examples of how the same rule can produce different silhouettes while still reading as part of one species.

In-world, **Multiple Tails** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: clothing openings at the waist, door clearance behind the body, balance while turning quickly, and sleeping without pinning the tail can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **Multiple Tails**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

In canon, multiple tails sits inside the same body-map logic as every other Noxivitre feature. It connects to body geometry, socket placement, balance, collision clearance, coordination, and BlackGlass-supported structural variation. The working substrate is the body map, skeletal or synthetic anchors, nerves, actuators, nanite bridges, and adaptive tissue around the changed body plan. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands multiple tails, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for multiple tails is a cool-looking design that has no room to move, duplicated structures that collide with each other, poor center of mass, or too many systems competing for the same space. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for multiple tails before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Multiple Tails** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Multiple Tails** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as the tail settling into a tighter resting curve and surface seams brightening during a correction should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For multiple tails, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Multiple Tails**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Multiple Tails** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, multiple tails matters through doors, chairs, beds, vehicles, hugs, carrying objects, sports, workspaces, and learning where every new body part is without staring at it. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note stance, gait, reach, turning radius, resting position, clothing cuts, furniture fit, and how the form looks when actually moving instead of posing. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of multiple tails so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Design a Common interpretation and a Mythic interpretation of the same idea.

- Decide what the nanites do when the feature is damaged.

- Write a version that is subtle enough to hide and another that cannot realistically be concealed.

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
**Multiple Tails** is one of those details that can look simple on a reference sheet and turn into a dozen small decisions the moment the character starts moving.

The useful questions here are **load paths, range of motion, proprioception, attachment or suspension logic, and the way nearby structures make room for it**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **Multiple Tails**, practical details can include sleeping without pinning the tail, balance while turning quickly, clothing openings at the waist, and seating and chair backs. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **Multiple Tails** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include positional drift behind the hips, numbness near the tail base, and delayed balance correction. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **Multiple Tails** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include the tail settling into a tighter resting curve, surface seams brightening during a correction, and visible nanite traffic at the base. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through clothing openings at the waist, seating and chair backs, and balance while turning quickly—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **Multiple Tails**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. The safest fallback is usually a mechanically conservative posture or reduced range, not the anatomy vanishing for no reason. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- How does **Multiple Tails** affect clothing, furniture, sleep, travel, or personal space?
- What would a Noxivitre medic see about **Multiple Tails** that an ordinary observer would miss?
- What is the first small sign that **Multiple Tails** is overloaded, damaged, or badly calibrated?
- Which parts of **Multiple Tails** are automatic, and which can be deliberately controlled?

#### Character-facing note

**Multiple Tails** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.

**PART V — MORPHOLOGY & TRAIT CATALOG • ENTRY 111 · [ATLAS](#nox_atlas) / [PART INDEX](#part-v-quick-index)**

# **Functional Wings**

Functional Wings is a morphology option rather than a mandatory species trait. It should still look BlackGlass-built: the joints, attachment points, floating gaps, plating, and mutation seams should make the feature feel native to the species instead of pasted on.

**GENERATION ZERO / THE FIRST PAIR**

Noxivitre history starts with two people rather than with a factory model or an ancient naturally occurring population. Riven Solace and Blade were originally Protogens, and neither one began life as a Noxivitre. Their conversion happened when BlackGlass stopped behaving like an outside contaminant or an unusual mutation source and became a permanent body-level rewrite system that their nanites, nerves, synthetic structures, and living tissue all had to organize around. Once that architecture stabilized, calling them mutated Protogens stopped being a complete biological description. The new classification was Noxivitre, the two of them became Generation Zero, and continued maturation eventually placed both founders in the creator-locked Unobtanium rarity.

Riven and Blade are treated as co-origins. There is no canon 'real first one' hidden between them unless future lore deliberately establishes a measurable difference of seconds or minutes, and even then the culture can still remember them as the First Pair. The species exists because the same BlackGlass event reached stable compatibility in both of them and produced a body architecture that could persist instead of burning itself out. Later researchers, communities, or descendants can argue over terminology, but the bible treats both names as equally foundational.

Riven's starting point was already unusual. Before full conversion he was an Uncommon Protogen with traits he normally concealed: his legs floated rather than physically joining the torso in the ordinary way, his tail was also a floating limb, he had horns, and he possessed two biological ear pairs. Those features matter because they predate Noxivitre classification. BlackGlass does not erase that history; it later reinterprets those existing structures through Noxivitre biology, surrounding the floating separations with active nanite bridges, threading the horns with BlackGlass-responsive sensory channels, and integrating both ear pairs into a much denser sensory map. Riven's conversion is therefore the complicated founder case: the body was already atypical before the species-defining rewrite began, and the rewrite grows around those traits instead of pretending they were created from nothing.

Blade gives the setting the opposite comparison. He began as a Common Protogen with a much more ordinary baseline, which makes changes produced by BlackGlass easier to isolate. As his conversion matures, the changes are therefore especially obvious: his once-continuous Protogen facial architecture develops into a mobile Fractureface, new BlackGlass plates begin to float independently around major joints, his tail gains controlled segmentation and temporary decoupling, and his nanites become capable of maintaining anatomy that did not exist anywhere in his original body plan. When broad Noxivitre systems appear in both founders despite their different starting bodies, it is strong evidence that the feature belongs to the new species rather than to Riven's old Uncommon traits.

Both founders eventually developed six full arms: their original pair plus two additional duplicated pairs. The duplicated arms followed each person's own anatomy, fur, plating, proportions, coloration, and mechanical-biological construction. They were not generic blue BlackGlass arms grafted onto the body. As the founders mature further, those six arms stop reading as a single mutation pasted onto a Protogen body and become part of a larger Noxivitre layout: shoulder and rib structures adapt to three independent arm pairs, BlackGlass channels redistribute load between sockets, floating support plates move out of the way automatically, and their body maps treat all six arms as equally native. This became one of the earliest rules of Noxivitre mutation biology: when BlackGlass has a healthy personal template available, it prefers to build from that person's body map. Mutation can be extreme without erasing who the body belongs to.

The founders are important, but they are not mandatory templates. A Noxivitre does not need six arms, floating legs, horns, multiple ears, pink coloration, white fur, a Protogen ancestry, or any exact trait from Riven or Blade. Their role is historical and mechanistic. They prove that BlackGlass can cross the line from mutation into a stable species architecture, they establish the first body-map precedents, and they provide the oldest known examples of nanites learning to maintain anatomy that did not exist in the original body.

Generation Zero status and rarity are conceptually separate, but Riven and Blade are explicitly Unobtanium. They are not Unobtanium merely because they came first, nor because six arms, floating anatomy, horns, or extreme mutations need to be locked away. They qualify because their mature Generation-Zero bodies develop Origin Glasshearts and founder-class body-map authoring: BlackGlass can establish new stable personal anatomy pathways rather than only expressing ordinary inherited or learned mutation patterns. Common through Mythic remain open tiers, and a Mythic character can be visually stranger, larger, or more complicated than either founder without becoming Unobtanium. The lock is tied to creator-approved canon architecture, not to making everyone else's designs less interesting.

### **OUT-OF-UNIVERSE CHARACTER OWNERSHIP**

Riven Solace is owned by @n4k2 on Discord. Blade is owned by @altblade on Discord. Those credits should stay attached to the characters when this bible is shared, excerpted, adapted, or expanded. The NOXIVITRES species is open through Mythic, but that openness is permission to create new Noxivitres, not permission to claim, redesign, or redistribute Riven or Blade.

### **MATURE GENERATION-ZERO DIVERGENCE**

Riven and Blade keep recognizable pieces of their former Protogen selves, but their mature bodies increasingly stop following Protogen architecture. Their facial displays separate into mobile BlackGlass Fractureface structures rather than one uninterrupted visor shell; plates can float around joints instead of remaining bolted to a fixed armor layout; Vitrite nanites become visible as connective fields during heavy movement; and both bodies acquire structures that exist because the Glassheart actively maintains them rather than because those structures were present in the original genome or chassis.

The change is deliberately gradual. There is no single second where every old feature vanishes and a completely unrelated creature appears. Instead, more and more of the body starts obeying Noxivitre rules until Protogen is useful only as ancestry. The six arms become fully native, facial architecture becomes fracture-based, BlackGlass channels replace ordinary fixed interfaces, and the founders gain personal mutation systems that can create new stable configurations without treating every change as damage.

Later Noxivitres can have several origins. Some may be Converted from compatible pre-existing species, some may be Glassborn with Noxivitre systems from the beginning, some may be deliberately Forged, and sufficiently developed BlackGlass colonies may eventually produce Emergent individuals. None of those origins replace the historical beginning. Riven and Blade remain the point at which the species first became real, stable, named, and repeatable enough that later Noxivitres could be recognized as members of the same biological family.

### **FOUNDATION RULES FROM GENERATION ZERO**

- Riven and Blade are both canonically first; neither is treated as a prototype owned by the other.

- Their former Protogen traits remain part of their personal history and can persist after conversion.

- BlackGlass duplication normally follows the individual’s own body template unless instability or corruption is specifically established.

- Six arms are a founder precedent, not a species requirement and not an Unobtanium-only feature.

- Founder status by itself does not equal rarity, power level, or social rank; Riven and Blade are specifically Unobtanium because their mature Generation-Zero core architecture carries founder-class, creator-locked BlackGlass functions.

- Later origins can expand the species without retconning Generation Zero.

**HOW TO USE THIS BIBLE**

This is meant to be a giant working reference, not a rulebook that makes people ask permission every five minutes. If you are designing a character, start with Part I, Part VI, and Part XI, then jump to whatever anatomy or mutation pages matter to that character.

If you are writing lore, treat the defaults as shared language. Exceptions are allowed when they have a reason. A weird exception is usually more interesting when everyone involved knows what the normal rule was first.

If you and your friends add new canon, write it so it answers at least one useful question: what does it look like, how does it work, what does it change for a character, or why does it matter to the setting. If it answers none of those, it can stay a fun headcanon until it grows into something stronger.

Most importantly, do not let the rarity chart eat the species. The BlackGlass body system, mutable anatomy, nanites, personal identity, and visual construction language are the actual species. Rarity is just a way to organize how extreme a design is.

| **SYSTEM**                       | **PRIMARY JOB**                                                                                          | **WHAT IT DOES NOT AUTOMATICALLY MEAN**                                            |
|----------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Glassheart**                   | Maintains the high-level body map, continuity rules, and large-scale coordination.                       | It is not a soul meter, rarity badge, or automatic power source for every ability. |
| **BlackGlass**                   | Living mutagenic construction material that can maintain, repair, detach, duplicate, or rewrite anatomy. | It does not make every mutation random, violent, evil, or uncontrollable.          |
| **Vitrite nanites**              | Fine-scale repair, signaling, scaffolding, local construction, diagnostics, and interface work.          | Nanites are not the entire organism and do not replace personality or biology.     |
| **Body map**                     | The current accepted structural definition of the individual.                                            | It is not a rigid blueprint; it can be revised and can contain temporary states.   |
| **Fractureface / facial system** | Cyber-organic expression, protection, sensory integration, and identity presentation.                    | A Noxivitre does not need to copy a Protogen visor silhouette.                     |
| **Rarity**                       | Describes overall structural/BlackGlass complexity and how extreme the stable design is.                 | Rarity is not social rank, moral worth, intelligence, or a universal combat tier.  |

## CANON LAYERS & CHANGE AUTHORITY

| **LAYER**                   | **MEANING**                                                                                       | **CHANGE RULE**                                                               |
|-----------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Species baseline**        | The short concept that should remain recognizable across almost every character.                  | Change cautiously; this is the identity layer.                                |
| **Working defaults**        | Common biological, visual, social, and technical assumptions used when no exception is specified. | Expandable; exceptions are allowed when explained.                            |
| **Character canon**         | Facts specific to one OC, including anatomy, relationships, history, and owner choices.           | Character owner takes priority for that character.                            |
| **Founder canon**           | Generation Zero facts tied specifically to Riven and Blade.                                       | Requires owner/creator approval; never infer ownership from species openness. |
| **Open-species permission** | What outside creators may use without asking.                                                     | Common through Mythic remain open; Unobtanium remains creator-locked.         |

# **ANATOMY REFERENCE**

A Noxivitre body is best understood as a coordinated stack of living tissue, synthetic structures, BlackGlass, nanites, and a persistent body map. Individual builds can omit, relocate, duplicate, detach, or heavily modify many visible structures without ceasing to be Noxivitres.

| **REGION / SYSTEM**   | **DEFAULT FUNCTION**                                                      | **COMMON VARIATION QUESTIONS**                                                   |
|-----------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Head / face**       | Expression, sensory housing, identity display, protection.                | Continuous vs segmented? Floating plates? Biological mouth? Exposed BlackGlass?  |
| **Glassheart region** | High-level body-map coordination and systemic stabilization.              | Single core, distributed support nodes, unusual placement, founder architecture? |
| **Arms / hands**      | Manipulation and interaction.                                             | 2, 4, 6, 8+? Symmetrical? Floating? Duplicated from original pair?               |
| **Legs / feet**       | Locomotion and posture.                                                   | Plantigrade, digitigrade, floating, segmented, temporarily decouplable?          |
| **Tail systems**      | Balance, communication, locomotion, storage, defense, or pure morphology. | Single/multiple? Floating? Aquatic? Draconic? Mechanical? Shape-changing?        |
| **Back / wings**      | Flight, display, heat management, stabilization, or storage.              | Functional vs decorative? One pair vs several? Organic vs BlackGlass-grown?      |
| **External plates**   | Protection and cyber-organic structure.                                   | Fixed, retractable, orbiting, fractured, translucent, grown only during stress?  |
| **Nanite reservoirs** | Store and distribute Vitrites.                                            | Centralized vs distributed? High-capacity? Specialized local strains?            |

| **GLASSSHIFT CLASS** | **SCOPE**                                                           | **TYPICAL EXAMPLES**                                                     | **MAIN DESIGN QUESTION**                                                |
|----------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Micro**            | Surface or local adjustment.                                        | Markings, claws, plate edges, eye/display changes, small sensory shifts. | Does it reset quickly or become the new default?                        |
| **Minor**            | One recognizable structure changes.                                 | Horn growth, tail alteration, local plating, limited detachment.         | How is coordination learned and stabilized?                             |
| **Major**            | Body plan changes meaningfully.                                     | New arm pair, floating legs, functional wings, torso restructuring.      | What else must move, reroute, or be rebuilt around it?                  |
| **Recursive**        | An existing structure becomes a reusable template.                  | Repeated limb duplication, mirrored plates, repeated sensory structures. | What prevents runaway copying or resource collapse?                     |
| **Systemic**         | Multiple systems revise together.                                   | Whole-body size shift, integrated face/core rewrite, major conversion.   | What preserves memory, identity, and continuity while the body changes? |
| **Founder-authored** | Generation-Zero body-map authoring rather than ordinary expression. | New stable pathways created by Riven/Blade founder architecture.         | Owner/creator approval; do not treat this as a generic Mythic ability.  |

| **STABILITY SIGNAL**            | **WHAT IT USUALLY MEANS**                                        | **STORY / MEDICAL RESPONSE**                                                   |
|---------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Clean synchronization**       | New structure moves naturally and matches the accepted body map. | Normal adaptation, training, clothing/equipment adjustment.                    |
| **Lag / ghost motion**          | Nanite or neural routing is slightly behind conscious intent.    | Rest, recalibration, local diagnostics, coordination practice.                 |
| **Flicker / plate drift**       | Local anchoring or expression geometry is unstable.              | Check nanite reserve, stress load, local BlackGlass integrity.                 |
| **Repeated unwanted reversion** | Body map and current structure disagree.                         | Determine which state the individual actually accepts as baseline.             |
| **Recursive overbuild**         | Duplication continues beyond intended endpoint.                  | Cut triggers, stabilize template boundaries, protect core resources.           |
| **Core desynchronization**      | Local body sections disagree with Glassheart high-level state.   | Medical priority; avoid forcing another major Glassshift until resynchronized. |

# **VITRITE NANITE REFERENCE**

| **ROLE**         | **LOCAL JOB**                                                    | **FAILURE LOOK**                                        | **NOTES**                                         |
|------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| **Signal**       | Carry timing, position, sensation, and coordination data.        | Lag, numbness, delayed floating-part response.          | Especially important in detached anatomy.         |
| **Scaffold**     | Hold temporary geometry while tissue/BlackGlass catches up.      | Visible particle haze, weak temporary structures.       | Can be temporary without being damage.            |
| **Repair**       | Close wounds, reconnect interfaces, rebuild small structures.    | Slow healing or incomplete surface finish.              | Does not erase consequences automatically.        |
| **Construction** | Assemble new plates, supports, duplicated anatomy, interfaces.   | Malformed edges, asymmetry, unfinished hard structures. | Works from body-map instructions.                 |
| **Diagnostic**   | Sample local state and report mismatches.                        | False alarms, missing data, delayed health feedback.    | Useful for medicine and self-monitoring.          |
| **Interface**    | Connect organic nerves, BlackGlass, synthetic components, tools. | Input jitter, tool rejection, sensory cross-talk.       | Allows highly integrated cyber-organic equipment. |

| **STAGE**                                | **BODY-MAP EMPHASIS**                                                                    | **COMMON STORY QUESTIONS**                                                       |
|------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Formation / conversion**               | Can the Glassheart and local systems agree on a stable identity/body baseline?           | What was retained? What was newly constructed? What feels natural vs learned?    |
| **Early synchronization**                | Coordination becomes reliable across organic, synthetic, BlackGlass, and nanite systems. | What movements feel strange? What needs training?                                |
| **First major Glassshift**               | The individual learns that their body can revise itself beyond repair.                   | Was it intentional, stress-triggered, developmental, or environmental?           |
| **Established adulthood / stable phase** | Mutable anatomy becomes part of routine life rather than a constant emergency.           | Clothes, housing, work, intimacy, maintenance, self-image.                       |
| **Later adaptation**                     | New states can be integrated without deleting prior identity.                            | What becomes permanent? What stays optional? What does the person actually want? |

# **SENSES, EXPRESSION & BODY LANGUAGE**

| **CHANNEL**                 | **CAN COMMUNICATE**                                                                      | **DESIGN NOTES**                                                                                                        |
|-----------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Fractureface**            | Eye shapes, symbols, mouth geometry, plate spacing, glitch-like transitions, brightness. | Expression can continue across separated plates; do not treat it as a flat screen unless that is the individual design. |
| **Ears / sensors**          | Attention, uncertainty, annoyance, fear, tracking, sensory focus.                        | Biological, synthetic, floating, multiple pairs, or absent.                                                             |
| **Tail(s)**                 | Balance, excitement, defensiveness, affection, agitation, locomotor intent.              | Multiple tails may communicate independently or as one coordinated display.                                             |
| **Wings / back structures** | Confidence, threat display, comfort, flight readiness, shielding.                        | Functional purpose and emotional signaling can coexist.                                                                 |
| **Nanite field**            | Stress shimmer, repair activity, intentional ornamentation, bridge visibility.           | Visible nanites are a readable body state, not automatically damage.                                                    |
| **BlackGlass plates**       | Tension, expansion, retraction, orbit distance, protective posture.                      | Plate movement should have clearance and a reason in the body map.                                                      |
| **Color / light**           | Mood accent, system status, deliberate styling.                                          | Avoid making color an infallible lie detector or morality signal.                                                       |

# **MEDICAL / TROUBLESHOOTING QUICK REFERENCE**

| **OBSERVATION**                               | **CHECK FIRST**                                                               | **DO NOT ASSUME**                                            |
|-----------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Floating limb drifts or lags**              | Nanite bridge signal, local reserve, sensory feedback, stress.                | That detachment itself is abnormal.                          |
| **New limb pair is clumsy**                   | Coordination learning, socket clearance, nervous routing, clothing collision. | The Glassshift failed just because control is not immediate. |
| **Face plates separate farther than usual**   | Emotion, protective state, sensory mode, local anchoring.                     | The face is "breaking."                                      |
| **BlackGlass keeps rebuilding removed trait** | Body map still considers the trait canonical.                                 | Cutting it off will permanently remove it.                   |
| **Repeated involuntary shifts**               | Triggers, stress, body-map disagreement, resource imbalance.                  | The character has no agency or is becoming evil.             |
| **Nanite haze increases**                     | Repair load, bridge load, construction, display, heat/resource management.    | Every visible swarm is contamination.                        |
| **Core activity spikes**                      | Large coordination demand, major shift, injury, emotional load.               | Rarity increased or an Unobtanium state activated.           |
