| **FIELD**              | **WRITE DOWN**                                                                                                  |
|------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Character / owner**  | Name, ownership credit, pronouns, age/context.                                                                  |
| **Origin**             | Glassborn, Converted, Forged, Emergent, or a justified setting-specific exception.                              |
| **Baseline anatomy**   | Height/build, stance, arm count, leg type, tails, ears, horns, wings, face structure.                           |
| **Glassheart**         | Location/architecture, stability, unusual nodes, any owner-approved special rules.                              |
| **BlackGlass pattern** | Where it is visible, what it can rewrite, common triggers, preferred stable form.                               |
| **Vitrites**           | Visible behavior, special local roles, bridge style, repair/construction habits.                                |
| **Rarity**             | Classify the entire build from Common through Mythic; Unobtanium requires explicit creator approval.            |
| **Daily consequences** | At least 3 mundane effects: clothing, furniture, movement, maintenance, privacy, work, sleep, etc.              |
| **Limits**             | At least 2 meaningful constraints or costs that keep abilities readable.                                        |
| **Character first**    | Goals, relationships, flaws, humor, fears, habits — things that matter even if every mutation scene is removed. |

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
The best way to understand **Functional Wings** is to imagine the character dealing with it on a boring Tuesday, not only during a transformation scene.

The useful questions here are **load paths, range of motion, proprioception, attachment or suspension logic, and the way nearby structures make room for it**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **Functional Wings**, practical details can include folding geometry while sitting, doorway and ceiling clearance, air load during fast movement, and keeping the wings from blocking people in crowded spaces. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **Functional Wings** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include loss of fine feather or membrane control, one wing locking into a safer folded state, and uneven extension. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **Functional Wings** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include a deliberate half-fold used as a resting posture, support seams becoming visible near the shoulder roots, and nanites reinforcing the leading edge. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through harness and clothing design, air load during fast movement, and doorway and ceiling clearance—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **Functional Wings**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. The safest fallback is usually a mechanically conservative posture or reduced range, not the anatomy vanishing for no reason. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- Does **Functional Wings** behave differently during a Glassshift, active repair, or emotional stress?
- What does **Functional Wings** feel like when nothing is wrong?
- How does **Functional Wings** affect clothing, furniture, sleep, travel, or personal space?
- What would a Noxivitre medic see about **Functional Wings** that an ordinary observer would miss?

#### Character-facing note

**Functional Wings** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.


**PART I — IDENTITY & FOUNDATION • ENTRY 001 · [ATLAS](#nox_atlas) / [PART INDEX](#part-i-quick-index)**
<a id="entry-001"></a>

# **The Species in One Sentence**

The Species in One Sentence helps define identity, boundaries, and the rules that keep the species recognizable without making every character identical. It is part of the baseline rather than a hard ceiling, so later lore can add detail without needing to throw out the whole species concept.

- Design around whether the trait can be voluntarily suppressed.

- Decide what clothing or equipment has to change around it.

- Account for how the individual learned to coordinate it.

- Extra anatomy needs room to move. Limb sockets, wings, tails, and floating pieces should be placed with actual posture and collision in mind.

- Unobtanium should remain special through lore and permission, not by banning ordinary creators from having fun anatomy.

In practice, this can show up through details like fractured or floating face plates, ear or horn structures that integrate with the skull rather than looking glued on, or temporary nanite scaffolding. None of those are mandatory; they are examples of how the same rule can produce different silhouettes while still reading as part of one species.

In-world, **The Species in One Sentence** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: movement, clothing, maintenance, and ordinary social interaction can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **The Species in One Sentence**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

For Noxivitres, the species in one sentence is treated as a real system rather than a decorative trait. It connects to shared identity, visual language, and canon boundary. The working substrate is the BlackGlass rewrite system and the body-map rules every Noxivitre carries. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands the species in one sentence, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for the species in one sentence is a definition that becomes so broad that the species stops being recognizable, or so narrow that people cannot make interesting characters. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for the species in one sentence before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **The Species in One Sentence** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **The Species in One Sentence** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as a more compact resting state and subtle BlackGlass seams should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For the species in one sentence, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **The Species in One Sentence**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **The Species in One Sentence** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, the species in one sentence matters through character identity, presentation, community expectations, and whether a person chooses to show or hide unusual traits. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note how another character can recognize a Noxivitre without relying on one exact silhouette. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception. Riven Solace and Blade are the canon reference point for the species in one sentence because they are Generation Zero: the first two Noxivitres. Riven entered that transition from an Uncommon Protogen baseline with concealed floating legs and tail, horns, and two ear pairs, while Blade entered from a much more ordinary Common Protogen baseline. Their different starting bodies make the pair unusually useful for separating inherited anatomy from genuinely Noxivitre-specific BlackGlass changes. When later lore is uncertain, the founders can be used as precedent without requiring every later Noxivitre to copy them.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of the species in one sentence so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Design a Common interpretation and a Mythic interpretation of the same idea.

- Decide what the nanites do when the feature is damaged.

- Describe how the feature changes clothing, furniture, movement, or sleeping posture.

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
For **The Species in One Sentence**, the species rules should answer the practical questions first and leave spectacle for when the story actually needs it.

The useful questions here are **sensory filtering, body ownership, attention, learned movement, memory continuity, and the difference between technical integration and emotional familiarity**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **The Species in One Sentence**, practical details can include sleep, maintenance, privacy, and movement. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **The Species in One Sentence** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include extra heat or energy use, temporary fallback behavior, and slower response. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **The Species in One Sentence** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include subtle BlackGlass seams, visible nanite traffic under load, and a more compact resting state. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through movement, ordinary social interaction, and clothing—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **The Species in One Sentence**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. The person’s sense of ownership matters. A technically healthy state can still feel wrong, and a strange-looking state can feel completely normal. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- What is the first small sign that **The Species in One Sentence** is overloaded, damaged, or badly calibrated?
- What does **The Species in One Sentence** feel like when nothing is wrong?
- How does **The Species in One Sentence** affect clothing, furniture, sleep, travel, or personal space?
- Which parts of **The Species in One Sentence** are automatic, and which can be deliberately controlled?

#### Character-facing note

**The Species in One Sentence** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.

The short version is useful, but **The Three-Sentence Baseline** becomes a lot easier to write once it is treated as part of somebody’s ordinary life.

# **What Makes the Species Its Own Thing**

The species is defined by mutable anatomy caused by BlackGlass, not by a visor, chest plate layout, or a fixed furry-cyborg ratio. If a design still reads as a Protogen with a different rarity chart, the design language needs another pass.

- Design around what maintenance the nanites perform.

- Decide what social assumptions are attached to it.

- Account for whether BlackGlass treats it as original anatomy or a later addition.

- Mutations should still obey the individual's body map unless the story explicitly establishes corruption or instability.

- A character can hide a trait without erasing it from their body map. Concealment is presentation, not nonexistence.

In practice, this can show up through details like organic fur interrupted by synthetic structures, distinctive paw or hand construction, or tails with visible mutation history. None of those are mandatory; they are examples of how the same rule can produce different silhouettes while still reading as part of one species.

In-world, **What Makes the Species Its Own Thing** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: maintenance, privacy, ordinary social interaction, and sleep can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **What Makes the Species Its Own Thing**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

In canon, what makes the species its own thing sits inside the same body-map logic as every other Noxivitre feature. It connects to shared identity, visual language, and canon boundary. The working substrate is the BlackGlass rewrite system and the body-map rules every Noxivitre carries. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands what makes the species its own thing, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for what makes the species its own thing is a definition that becomes so broad that the species stops being recognizable, or so narrow that people cannot make interesting characters. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for what makes the species its own thing before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **What Makes the Species Its Own Thing** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **What Makes the Species Its Own Thing** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as a more compact resting state and visible nanite traffic under load should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For what makes the species its own thing, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

# **BlackGlass as the Defining System**

BlackGlass as the Defining System helps define identity, boundaries, and the rules that keep the species recognizable without making every character identical. It is part of the baseline rather than a hard ceiling, so later lore can add detail without needing to throw out the whole species concept.

- Design around whether BlackGlass treats it as original anatomy or a later addition.

- Decide what the trait looks like when the individual is exhausted.

- Account for what clothing or equipment has to change around it.

- Extra anatomy needs room to move. Limb sockets, wings, tails, and floating pieces should be placed with actual posture and collision in mind.

- If a trait is copied from another species concept, change its construction and reason for existing so it fits BlackGlass biology.

In practice, this can show up through details like fractured or floating face plates, organic fur interrupted by synthetic structures, or tails with visible mutation history. None of those are mandatory; they are examples of how the same rule can produce different silhouettes while still reading as part of one species.

In-world, **BlackGlass as the Defining System** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: maintenance, ordinary social interaction, clothing, and privacy can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **BlackGlass as the Defining System**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

A useful way to understand blackglass as the defining system is to separate what the character sees from what BlackGlass and the nanites are actually doing underneath. It connects to mutation triggers, body-map rewriting, stabilization, and long-term mutation memory. The working substrate is active BlackGlass, dormant BlackGlass, Vitrite support swarms, core signaling, and the individual’s existing anatomy template. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands blackglass as the defining system, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for blackglass as the defining system is runaway rewriting, rejection, contradictory body maps, incomplete stabilization, or a Glassshift that keeps trying to solve a problem after the problem is gone. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for blackglass as the defining system before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **BlackGlass as the Defining System** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **BlackGlass as the Defining System** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as visible nanite traffic under load and a more compact resting state should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For blackglass as the defining system, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **BlackGlass as the Defining System**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **BlackGlass as the Defining System** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, blackglass as the defining system matters through how someone plans around stress, repairs, medical scans, accidental triggers, body changes, and the possibility that yesterday’s anatomy is not exactly today’s. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note what changes first, what stays recognizable, how quickly the change stabilizes, and what evidence remains after the event. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception. Riven Solace and Blade are the canon reference point for blackglass as the defining system because they are Generation Zero: the first two Noxivitres. Riven entered that transition from an Uncommon Protogen baseline with concealed floating legs and tail, horns, and two ear pairs, while Blade entered from a much more ordinary Common Protogen baseline. Their different starting bodies make the pair unusually useful for separating inherited anatomy from genuinely Noxivitre-specific BlackGlass changes. When later lore is uncertain, the founders can be used as precedent without requiring every later Noxivitre to copy them.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of blackglass as the defining system so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Write one example of the trait on a calm character and one on a stressed character.

- Define what a medical scanner would call this feature.

- Decide whether the feature is congenital, constructed, acquired, or the result of a later Glassshift.

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
**BlackGlass as the Defining System** is one of those details that can look simple on a reference sheet and turn into a dozen small decisions the moment the character starts moving.

The useful questions here are **the accepted body map, Glassheart arbitration, rewrite state, material supply, and the point where a temporary change becomes stable anatomy**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **BlackGlass as the Defining System**, practical details can include privacy, maintenance, movement, and ordinary social interaction. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **BlackGlass as the Defining System** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include reduced precision, extra heat or energy use, and slower response. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **BlackGlass as the Defining System** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include subtle BlackGlass seams, visible nanite traffic under load, and a more compact resting state. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through ordinary social interaction, maintenance, and sleep—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **BlackGlass as the Defining System**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. A failed rewrite can stop at a stable intermediate state; the system would rather pause than keep changing blindly. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

When a later writer expands a body that is never completely fixed, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for a body that is never completely fixed is a definition that becomes so broad that the species stops being recognizable, or so narrow that people cannot make interesting characters. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for a body that is never completely fixed before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **A Body That Is Never Completely Fixed** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **A Body That Is Never Completely Fixed** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as subtle BlackGlass seams and a more compact resting state should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For a body that is never completely fixed, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **A Body That Is Never Completely Fixed**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **A Body That Is Never Completely Fixed** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, a body that is never completely fixed matters through character identity, presentation, community expectations, and whether a person chooses to show or hide unusual traits. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note how another character can recognize a Noxivitre without relying on one exact silhouette. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception. Riven Solace and Blade are the canon reference point for a body that is never completely fixed because they are Generation Zero: the first two Noxivitres. Riven entered that transition from an Uncommon Protogen baseline with concealed floating legs and tail, horns, and two ear pairs, while Blade entered from a much more ordinary Common Protogen baseline. Their different starting bodies make the pair unusually useful for separating inherited anatomy from genuinely Noxivitre-specific BlackGlass changes. When later lore is uncertain, the founders can be used as precedent without requiring every later Noxivitre to copy them.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of a body that is never completely fixed so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Decide whether the feature is congenital, constructed, acquired, or the result of a later Glassshift.

- Describe how the feature changes clothing, furniture, movement, or sleeping posture.

- Design a Common interpretation and a Mythic interpretation of the same idea.

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
The short version is useful, but **A Body That Is Never Completely Fixed** becomes a lot easier to write once it is treated as part of somebody’s ordinary life.

The useful questions here are **load paths, range of motion, proprioception, attachment or suspension logic, and the way nearby structures make room for it**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **A Body That Is Never Completely Fixed**, practical details can include sleep, privacy, movement, and ordinary social interaction. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **A Body That Is Never Completely Fixed** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include slower response, reduced precision, and extra heat or energy use. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **A Body That Is Never Completely Fixed** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include a more compact resting state, visible nanite traffic under load, and subtle BlackGlass seams. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through ordinary social interaction, sleep, and movement—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **A Body That Is Never Completely Fixed**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. The safest fallback is usually a mechanically conservative posture or reduced range, not the anatomy vanishing for no reason. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- Which parts of **A Body That Is Never Completely Fixed** are automatic, and which can be deliberately controlled?
- What is the first small sign that **A Body That Is Never Completely Fixed** is overloaded, damaged, or badly calibrated?
- What misconception about **A Body That Is Never Completely Fixed** would the character be tired of correcting?
- What does **A Body That Is Never Completely Fixed** feel like when nothing is wrong?

#### Character-facing note

**A Body That Is Never Completely Fixed** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.

For **Stable Versus Unstable Anatomy**, the species rules should answer the practical questions first and leave spectacle for when the story actually needs it.

With **Stable Versus Unstable Anatomy**, practical details can include movement, ordinary social interaction, clothing, and privacy. If a character breaks the normal version of **Stable Versus Unstable Anatomy**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

# **Individuality as a Species Rule**

Individuality as a Species Rule helps define identity, boundaries, and the rules that keep the species recognizable without making every character identical. It is part of the baseline rather than a hard ceiling, so later lore can add detail without needing to throw out the whole species concept.

- Design around whether BlackGlass treats it as original anatomy or a later addition.

- Decide what maintenance the nanites perform.

- Account for what emotional states make it more noticeable.

- Damage and mutation are different states. A missing part is not automatically a new trait, and a new trait is not automatically an injury.

- The open tiers should stay genuinely open. Do not quietly move popular traits into Unobtanium just to make them exclusive later.

In practice, this can show up through details like layered cybernetic joints, glowing nanite channels, or moving surface patterns that react to emotion. None of those are mandatory; they are examples of how the same rule can produce different silhouettes while still reading as part of one species.

In-world, **Individuality as a Species Rule** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: movement, sleep, ordinary social interaction, and privacy can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **Individuality as a Species Rule**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

The important thing about individuality as a species rule is that it has to work inside a mutable Noxivitre body, not only look good in a reference sheet. It connects to shared identity, visual language, and canon boundary. The working substrate is the BlackGlass rewrite system and the body-map rules every Noxivitre carries. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands individuality as a species rule, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for individuality as a species rule is a definition that becomes so broad that the species stops being recognizable, or so narrow that people cannot make interesting characters. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for individuality as a species rule before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Individuality as a Species Rule** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Individuality as a Species Rule** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as a more compact resting state and visible nanite traffic under load should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For individuality as a species rule, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Individuality as a Species Rule**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. - Write at least one mundane consequence of individuality as a species rule so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Decide whether the feature changes rarity by itself or only when combined with other major traits.

- Give the trait one practical downside that is not just 'it hurts.'

In practice, this can show up through details like subtle glitching around active mutations, layered cybernetic joints, or secondary sensory structures. None of those are mandatory; they are examples of how the same rule can produce different silhouettes while still reading as part of one species.

In-world, **No Required Gender or Personality** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: clothing, ordinary social interaction, movement, and privacy can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **No Required Gender or Personality**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

A useful way to understand no required gender or personality is to separate what the character sees from what BlackGlass and the nanites are actually doing underneath. It connects to perception, proprioception, emotional expression, sensory filtering, and the way cyber-organic anatomy is represented in the mind. The working substrate is biological nerves, synthetic signal paths, nanite relays, memory systems, facial displays, and the internal body map. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands no required gender or personality, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for no required gender or personality is sensory overload, phantom signals, delayed proprioception, mismatched expression, pain loops, or too much raw information arriving without useful filtering. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for no required gender or personality before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **No Required Gender or Personality** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **No Required Gender or Personality** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as subtle BlackGlass seams and visible nanite traffic under load should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For no required gender or personality, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **No Required Gender or Personality**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **No Required Gender or Personality** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, no required gender or personality matters through conversation, touch, sleep, stress, embarrassment, excitement, concentration, movement, and all the small body-language habits that make two Noxivitres feel completely different. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note what the individual actually feels, notices, ignores, expresses automatically, and has to consciously control. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of no required gender or personality so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Give the trait one practical downside that is not just 'it hurts.'

- Describe how the feature changes clothing, furniture, movement, or sleeping posture.

- Write one example of the trait on a calm character and one on a stressed character.

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
**No Required Gender or Personality** is one of those details that can look simple on a reference sheet and turn into a dozen small decisions the moment the character starts moving.

The useful questions here are **sensory filtering, body ownership, attention, learned movement, memory continuity, and the difference between technical integration and emotional familiarity**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **No Required Gender or Personality**, practical details can include sleep, privacy, movement, and clothing. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **No Required Gender or Personality** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include reduced precision, temporary fallback behavior, and slower response. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **No Required Gender or Personality** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include a more compact resting state, visible nanite traffic under load, and subtle BlackGlass seams. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through privacy, sleep, and movement—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **No Required Gender or Personality**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. The person’s sense of ownership matters. A technically healthy state can still feel wrong, and a strange-looking state can feel completely normal. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- What does **No Required Gender or Personality** feel like when nothing is wrong?
- What would a Noxivitre medic see about **No Required Gender or Personality** that an ordinary observer would miss?
- What misconception about **No Required Gender or Personality** would the character be tired of correcting?
- Which parts of **No Required Gender or Personality** are automatic, and which can be deliberately controlled?

#### Character-facing note

**No Required Gender or Personality** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.

- Give the feature a visual tell that becomes obvious during a Glassshift.

- Design a Common interpretation and a Mythic interpretation of the same idea.

- Decide whether the feature changes rarity by itself or only when combined with other major traits.

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
A good version of **Canon Versus Personal Headcanon** feels specific to the person wearing it. The system can be technically complicated without making the character talk like a manual.

With **Canon Versus Personal Headcanon**, practical details can include ordinary social interaction, clothing, movement, and maintenance. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **Canon Versus Personal Headcanon** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include extra heat or energy use, slower response, and temporary fallback behavior. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **Canon Versus Personal Headcanon** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include subtle BlackGlass seams, a more compact resting state, and visible nanite traffic under load. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through ordinary social interaction, privacy, and maintenance—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **Canon Versus Personal Headcanon**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

- Which parts of **Canon Versus Personal Headcanon** are automatic, and which can be deliberately controlled?

# **Creator Authority and Community Expansion**

Creator Authority and Community Expansion helps define identity, boundaries, and the rules that keep the species recognizable without making every character identical. It is part of the baseline rather than a hard ceiling, so later lore can add detail without needing to throw out the whole species concept.

- Design around what emotional states make it more noticeable.

- Decide how the individual learned to coordinate it.

- Account for whether the trait can be voluntarily suppressed.

- Mutations should still obey the individual's body map unless the story explicitly establishes corruption or instability.

- Extra anatomy needs room to move. Limb sockets, wings, tails, and floating pieces should be placed with actual posture and collision in mind.

In practice, this can show up through details like tails with visible mutation history, nonuniform crystalline surfaces, or distinctive paw or hand construction. None of those are mandatory; they are examples of how the same rule can produce different silhouettes while still reading as part of one species.

In-world, **Creator Authority and Community Expansion** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: sleep, privacy, clothing, and movement can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **Creator Authority and Community Expansion**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

A useful way to understand creator authority and community expansion is to separate what the character sees from what BlackGlass and the nanites are actually doing underneath. It connects to social meaning, consent, accommodation, community variation, and the ways people build traditions around mutable bodies without requiring one universal culture. The working substrate is families, friend groups, local communities, institutions, art, clothing, medicine, shared terminology, and personal choices. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands creator authority and community expansion, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for creator authority and community expansion is turning one community’s habit into a biological law, treating rarity as caste, ignoring bodily autonomy, or assuming every Noxivitre has the same attitude toward mutation. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for creator authority and community expansion before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Creator Authority and Community Expansion** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Creator Authority and Community Expansion** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as visible nanite traffic under load and a more compact resting state should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For creator authority and community expansion, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Creator Authority and Community Expansion**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of creator authority and community expansion so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Decide whether the feature changes rarity by itself or only when combined with other major traits.

- Give the feature a visual tell that becomes obvious during a Glassshift.
