# **Environmental Mutation**

Environmental Mutation describes one way BlackGlass changes, protects, or destabilizes a body. The important rule is that BlackGlass uses an internal body map, so even bizarre changes usually have a readable cause and a consistent anatomical result.

- Design around how it changes balance and movement.

- Decide whether BlackGlass treats it as original anatomy or a later addition.

- Account for what the trait looks like when the individual is exhausted.

- The species can be dramatic without making every member equally powerful. Anatomy, social rarity, and combat capability are separate things.

- If a trait is copied from another species concept, change its construction and reason for existing so it fits BlackGlass biology.

In practice, this can show up through details like moving surface patterns that react to emotion, body segments held together by a nanite bridge, or temporary nanite scaffolding. None of those are mandatory; they are examples of how the same rule can produce different silhouettes while still reading as part of one species.

In-world, **Environmental Mutation** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: maintenance, movement, privacy, and clothing can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **Environmental Mutation**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

For Noxivitres, environmental mutation is treated as a real system rather than a decorative trait. It connects to mutation triggers, body-map rewriting, stabilization, and long-term mutation memory. The working substrate is active BlackGlass, dormant BlackGlass, Vitrite support swarms, core signaling, and the individual’s existing anatomy template. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands environmental mutation, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for environmental mutation is runaway rewriting, rejection, contradictory body maps, incomplete stabilization, or a Glassshift that keeps trying to solve a problem after the problem is gone. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for environmental mutation before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Environmental Mutation** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Environmental Mutation** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as subtle BlackGlass seams and a more compact resting state should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For environmental mutation, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Environmental Mutation**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Environmental Mutation** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, environmental mutation matters through how someone plans around stress, repairs, medical scans, accidental triggers, body changes, and the possibility that yesterday’s anatomy is not exactly today’s. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note what changes first, what stays recognizable, how quickly the change stabilizes, and what evidence remains after the event. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of environmental mutation so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Define what a medical scanner would call this feature.

- Decide what the nanites do when the feature is damaged.

- Describe how the feature changes clothing, furniture, movement, or sleeping posture.

# **Nanite Swarm Behavior**

Nanite Swarm Behavior sits on the nanite/cybernetic side of the species. It exists to make the body function, communicate, repair itself, or control structures that ordinary nerves and muscles could not handle alone.

- Design around whether the body can rebuild it from a stored template.

- Decide what the trait looks like when the individual is exhausted.

- Account for how the individual learned to coordinate it.

- A cool visual does not automatically need a higher rarity; rarity should track structural complexity, not color or fashion.

- Mutations should still obey the individual's body map unless the story explicitly establishes corruption or instability.

In practice, this can show up through details like organic fur interrupted by synthetic structures, detached but synchronized anatomy, or distinctive paw or hand construction. None of those are mandatory; they are examples of how the same rule can produce different silhouettes while still reading as part of one species.

In-world, **Nanite Swarm Behavior** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: reaching across the torso without self-collision, sleeve and jacket construction, deciding which hands carry weight, and shoulder clearance can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **Nanite Swarm Behavior**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

A useful way to understand nanite swarm behavior is to separate what the character sees from what BlackGlass and the nanites are actually doing underneath. It connects to nanite command hierarchy, swarm behavior, repair logic, signal routing, and cybernetic integration. The working substrate is personal Vitrite strains, local swarm clusters, Glassheart instructions, stored body-map data, and power reserves. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands nanite swarm behavior, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for nanite swarm behavior is swarm exhaustion, command conflicts, corrupted templates, poor bandwidth, bad calibration, or too many simultaneous repair and mutation tasks. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Which parts of **Nanite Repair** are automatic, and which can be deliberately controlled?
- How does **Nanite Repair** affect clothing, furniture, sleep, travel, or personal space?
- What does **Nanite Repair** feel like when nothing is wrong?

#### Character-facing note

**Nanite Repair** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.


**PART IV — NANITES & CYBERNETICS • ENTRY 081 · [ATLAS](#nox_atlas) / [PART INDEX](#part-iv-quick-index)**

# **Nanite Construction**

Nanite Construction sits on the nanite/cybernetic side of the species. It exists to make the body function, communicate, repair itself, or control structures that ordinary nerves and muscles could not handle alone.

- Design around what social assumptions are attached to it.

- Decide what happens when the trait is damaged.

- Account for what clothing or equipment has to change around it.

- Extra anatomy needs room to move. Limb sockets, wings, tails, and floating pieces should be placed with actual posture and collision in mind.

- Damage and mutation are different states. A missing part is not automatically a new trait, and a new trait is not automatically an injury.

In practice, this can show up through details like asymmetrical glass growths, body segments held together by a nanite bridge, or subtle glitching around active mutations. None of those are mandatory; they are examples of how the same rule can produce different silhouettes while still reading as part of one species.

In-world, **Nanite Construction** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: privacy, movement, maintenance, and ordinary social interaction can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **Nanite Construction**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

For Noxivitres, nanite construction is treated as a real system rather than a decorative trait. It connects to nanite command hierarchy, swarm behavior, repair logic, signal routing, and cybernetic integration. The working substrate is personal Vitrite strains, local swarm clusters, Glassheart instructions, stored body-map data, and power reserves. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands nanite construction, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for nanite construction is swarm exhaustion, command conflicts, corrupted templates, poor bandwidth, bad calibration, or too many simultaneous repair and mutation tasks. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for nanite construction before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Nanite Construction** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Nanite Construction** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as visible nanite traffic under load and subtle BlackGlass seams should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For nanite construction, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Nanite Construction**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Nanite Construction** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, nanite construction matters through charging or feeding routines, maintenance, device interaction, privacy, repairs, sensory filtering, and the tiny automatic corrections the swarm performs constantly. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note response speed, visible particle behavior, heat, power use, repair quality, and whether a system can keep working when part of the body is physically separated. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of nanite construction so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Decide whether the feature changes rarity by itself or only when combined with other major traits.

- Decide whether the feature is congenital, constructed, acquired, or the result of a later Glassshift.

- Write a version that is subtle enough to hide and another that cannot realistically be concealed.

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
A good version of **Nanite Construction** feels specific to the person wearing it. The system can be technically complicated without making the character talk like a manual.

The useful questions here are **local swarm authority, bandwidth, reservoir access, signal routing, heat, and what the Vitrites are allowed to change without asking the Glassheart**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **Nanite Construction**, practical details can include ordinary social interaction, movement, clothing, and sleep. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **Nanite Construction** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include slower response, temporary fallback behavior, and reduced precision. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **Nanite Construction** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include subtle BlackGlass seams, a more compact resting state, and visible nanite traffic under load. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through maintenance, movement, and sleep—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **Nanite Construction**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. Local function can survive degraded network contact, but precision and repair speed usually drop before basic survival does. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- What would a Noxivitre medic see about **Nanite Construction** that an ordinary observer would miss?
- Which parts of **Nanite Construction** are automatic, and which can be deliberately controlled?
- What does **Nanite Construction** feel like when nothing is wrong?
- What is the first small sign that **Nanite Construction** is overloaded, damaged, or badly calibrated?

#### Character-facing note

**Nanite Construction** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.

# **Digital Expression Systems**

Digital Expression Systems sits on the nanite/cybernetic side of the species. It exists to make the body function, communicate, repair itself, or control structures that ordinary nerves and muscles could not handle alone.

- Design around whether the body can rebuild it from a stored template.

- Decide what social assumptions are attached to it.

- Account for whether the trait is hidden, visible, or selectively revealed.

- Damage and mutation are different states. A missing part is not automatically a new trait, and a new trait is not automatically an injury.

- Unobtanium should remain special through lore and permission, not by banning ordinary creators from having fun anatomy.

In practice, this can show up through details like layered cybernetic joints, fractured or floating face plates, or ear or horn structures that integrate with the skull rather than looking glued on. None of those are mandatory; they are examples of how the same rule can produce different silhouettes while still reading as part of one species.

In-world, **Digital Expression Systems** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: clothing, privacy, maintenance, and ordinary social interaction can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **Digital Expression Systems**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

For Noxivitres, digital expression systems is treated as a real system rather than a decorative trait. It connects to nanite command hierarchy, swarm behavior, repair logic, signal routing, and cybernetic integration. The working substrate is personal Vitrite strains, local swarm clusters, Glassheart instructions, stored body-map data, and power reserves. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands digital expression systems, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for digital expression systems is swarm exhaustion, command conflicts, corrupted templates, poor bandwidth, bad calibration, or too many simultaneous repair and mutation tasks. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for digital expression systems before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Digital Expression Systems** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Digital Expression Systems** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as a more compact resting state and visible nanite traffic under load should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For digital expression systems, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

# **Non-Visor Face Alternatives**

Non-Visor Face Alternatives sits on the nanite/cybernetic side of the species. It exists to make the body function, communicate, repair itself, or control structures that ordinary nerves and muscles could not handle alone.

- Design around what the trait looks like when the individual is exhausted.

- Decide what happens when the trait is damaged.

- Account for whether the trait can be voluntarily suppressed.

- Damage and mutation are different states. A missing part is not automatically a new trait, and a new trait is not automatically an injury.

- A character can hide a trait without erasing it from their body map. Concealment is presentation, not nonexistence.

In practice, this can show up through details like asymmetrical glass growths, secondary sensory structures, or tails with visible mutation history. None of those are mandatory; they are examples of how the same rule can produce different silhouettes while still reading as part of one species.

In-world, **Non-Visor Face Alternatives** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: glare control, impact protection, cleaning seams between plates, and facial expression can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **Non-Visor Face Alternatives**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

In canon, non-visor face alternatives sits inside the same body-map logic as every other Noxivitre feature. It connects to nanite command hierarchy, swarm behavior, repair logic, signal routing, and cybernetic integration. The working substrate is personal Vitrite strains, local swarm clusters, Glassheart instructions, stored body-map data, and power reserves. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands non-visor face alternatives, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for non-visor face alternatives is swarm exhaustion, command conflicts, corrupted templates, poor bandwidth, bad calibration, or too many simultaneous repair and mutation tasks. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for non-visor face alternatives before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Non-Visor Face Alternatives** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Non-Visor Face Alternatives** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as nanites sweeping across scratches during repair and status elements dimming when tired should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For non-visor face alternatives, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Non-Visor Face Alternatives**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Non-Visor Face Alternatives** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, non-visor face alternatives matters through charging or feeding routines, maintenance, device interaction, privacy, repairs, sensory filtering, and the tiny automatic corrections the swarm performs constantly. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note response speed, visible particle behavior, heat, power use, repair quality, and whether a system can keep working when part of the body is physically separated. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of non-visor face alternatives so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Voice Modulation**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Voice Modulation** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, voice modulation matters through charging or feeding routines, maintenance, device interaction, privacy, repairs, sensory filtering, and the tiny automatic corrections the swarm performs constantly. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note response speed, visible particle behavior, heat, power use, repair quality, and whether a system can keep working when part of the body is physically separated. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of voice modulation so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Write a version that is subtle enough to hide and another that cannot realistically be concealed.

- Write one example of the trait on a calm character and one on a stressed character.

- Design a Common interpretation and a Mythic interpretation of the same idea.

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
**Voice Modulation** is one of those details that can look simple on a reference sheet and turn into a dozen small decisions the moment the character starts moving.

The useful questions here are **local swarm authority, bandwidth, reservoir access, signal routing, heat, and what the Vitrites are allowed to change without asking the Glassheart**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **Voice Modulation**, practical details can include speaking while damaged, accent and personal speech habits, microphone compatibility, and deciding when modulation is expressive versus automatic. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **Voice Modulation** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include reduced volume, digital artifacts, and fallback to an unprocessed baseline voice. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **Voice Modulation** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include nanite stabilization after vocal strain, brief waveform displays, and throat or facial interfaces pulsing with speech. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through deciding when modulation is expressive versus automatic, accent and personal speech habits, and microphone compatibility—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **Voice Modulation**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. Local function can survive degraded network contact, but precision and repair speed usually drop before basic survival does. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- What misconception about **Voice Modulation** would the character be tired of correcting?
- What would a Noxivitre medic see about **Voice Modulation** that an ordinary observer would miss?
- What is the first small sign that **Voice Modulation** is overloaded, damaged, or badly calibrated?
- Which parts of **Voice Modulation** are automatic, and which can be deliberately controlled?

#### Character-facing note

**Voice Modulation** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. # **Internal Networking**

Internal Networking sits on the nanite/cybernetic side of the species. It exists to make the body function, communicate, repair itself, or control structures that ordinary nerves and muscles could not handle alone.

- Design around how it changes balance and movement.

- Decide what social assumptions are attached to it.

- Account for how the individual learned to coordinate it.

- Extra anatomy needs room to move. Limb sockets, wings, tails, and floating pieces should be placed with actual posture and collision in mind.

- A cool visual does not automatically need a higher rarity; rarity should track structural complexity, not color or fashion.

In practice, this can show up through details like detached but synchronized anatomy, secondary sensory structures, or ear or horn structures that integrate with the skull rather than looking glued on. None of those are mandatory; they are examples of how the same rule can produce different silhouettes while still reading as part of one species.

In-world, **Internal Networking** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: maintenance, movement, ordinary social interaction, and clothing can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **Internal Networking**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

A useful way to understand internal networking is to separate what the character sees from what BlackGlass and the nanites are actually doing underneath. It connects to nanite command hierarchy, swarm behavior, repair logic, signal routing, and cybernetic integration. The working substrate is personal Vitrite strains, local swarm clusters, Glassheart instructions, stored body-map data, and power reserves. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands internal networking, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for internal networking is swarm exhaustion, command conflicts, corrupted templates, poor bandwidth, bad calibration, or too many simultaneous repair and mutation tasks. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for internal networking before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Internal Networking** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Internal Networking** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as visible nanite traffic under load and a more compact resting state should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For internal networking, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

**PART IV — NANITES & CYBERNETICS • ENTRY 095 · [ATLAS](#nox_atlas) / [PART INDEX](#part-iv-quick-index)**

# **External Device Interfaces**

External Device Interfaces sits on the nanite/cybernetic side of the species. It exists to make the body function, communicate, repair itself, or control structures that ordinary nerves and muscles could not handle alone.

- Design around how medical scans classify it.

- Decide what clothing or equipment has to change around it.

- Account for whether the trait is hidden, visible, or selectively revealed.

- BlackGlass can be weird without being random. Repeated motifs, copied anatomy, and consistent nanite behavior make extreme designs feel intentional.

- Extra anatomy needs room to move. Limb sockets, wings, tails, and floating pieces should be placed with actual posture and collision in mind.

In practice, this can show up through details like body segments held together by a nanite bridge, duplicated limb sockets that follow real body mechanics, or visible BlackGlass seams. None of those are mandatory; they are examples of how the same rule can produce different silhouettes while still reading as part of one species.

In-world, **External Device Interfaces** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: eating and drinking, impact protection, facial expression, and privacy around diagnostic displays can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **External Device Interfaces**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

A useful way to understand external device interfaces is to separate what the character sees from what BlackGlass and the nanites are actually doing underneath. It connects to nanite command hierarchy, swarm behavior, repair logic, signal routing, and cybernetic integration. The working substrate is personal Vitrite strains, local swarm clusters, Glassheart instructions, stored body-map data, and power reserves. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands external device interfaces, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for external device interfaces is swarm exhaustion, command conflicts, corrupted templates, poor bandwidth, bad calibration, or too many simultaneous repair and mutation tasks. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for external device interfaces before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **External Device Interfaces** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **External Device Interfaces** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as plates separating slightly during strong emotion and a display simplifying when processing load rises should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For external device interfaces, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **External Device Interfaces**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **External Device Interfaces** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, external device interfaces matters through charging or feeding routines, maintenance, device interaction, privacy, repairs, sensory filtering, and the tiny automatic corrections the swarm performs constantly. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note response speed, visible particle behavior, heat, power use, repair quality, and whether a system can keep working when part of the body is physically separated. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of external device interfaces so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Describe how the feature changes clothing, furniture, movement, or sleeping posture.

- Decide what the nanites do when the feature is damaged.

- Give the feature a visual tell that becomes obvious during a Glassshift.

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
The best way to understand **External Device Interfaces** is to imagine the character dealing with it on a boring Tuesday, not only during a transformation scene.

The useful questions here are **local swarm authority, bandwidth, reservoir access, signal routing, heat, and what the Vitrites are allowed to change without asking the Glassheart**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **External Device Interfaces**, practical details can include eating and drinking, impact protection, facial expression, and privacy around diagnostic displays. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **External Device Interfaces** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include one plate locking in place, expression lag, and reduced jaw or facial range until calibration completes. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **External Device Interfaces** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include internal light visible through seams, plates separating slightly during strong emotion, and a display simplifying when processing load rises. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through eating and drinking, cleaning seams between plates, and facial expression—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **External Device Interfaces**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. Local function can survive degraded network contact, but precision and repair speed usually drop before basic survival does. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- Does **External Device Interfaces** behave differently during a Glassshift, active repair, or emotional stress?
- What misconception about **External Device Interfaces** would the character be tired of correcting?
- What does **External Device Interfaces** feel like when nothing is wrong?
- How does **External Device Interfaces** affect clothing, furniture, sleep, travel, or personal space?

#### Character-facing note

**External Device Interfaces** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.

# **Decorative Wings**

Decorative Wings is a morphology option rather than a mandatory species trait. It should still look BlackGlass-built: the joints, attachment points, floating gaps, plating, and mutation seams should make the feature feel native to the species instead of pasted on.

- Design around what happens when the trait is damaged.

- Decide what social assumptions are attached to it.

- Account for what the trait looks like when the individual is exhausted.

- Mutations should still obey the individual's body map unless the story explicitly establishes corruption or instability.

- Damage and mutation are different states. A missing part is not automatically a new trait, and a new trait is not automatically an injury.

In practice, this can show up through details like visible core-light through translucent BlackGlass, fractured or floating face plates, or moving surface patterns that react to emotion. None of those are mandatory; they are examples of how the same rule can produce different silhouettes while still reading as part of one species.

In-world, **Decorative Wings** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: air load during fast movement, keeping the wings from blocking people in crowded spaces, harness and clothing design, and doorway and ceiling clearance can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **Decorative Wings**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

For Noxivitres, decorative wings is treated as a real system rather than a decorative trait. It connects to body geometry, socket placement, balance, collision clearance, coordination, and BlackGlass-supported structural variation. The working substrate is the body map, skeletal or synthetic anchors, nerves, actuators, nanite bridges, and adaptive tissue around the changed body plan. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands decorative wings, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for decorative wings is a cool-looking design that has no room to move, duplicated structures that collide with each other, poor center of mass, or too many systems competing for the same space. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for decorative wings before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Decorative Wings** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Decorative Wings** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as nanites reinforcing the leading edge and a deliberate half-fold used as a resting posture should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For decorative wings, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Decorative Wings**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Decorative Wings** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, decorative wings matters through doors, chairs, beds, vehicles, hugs, carrying objects, sports, workspaces, and learning where every new body part is without staring at it. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note stance, gait, reach, turning radius, resting position, clothing cuts, furniture fit, and how the form looks when actually moving instead of posing. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of decorative wings so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Write a version that is subtle enough to hide and another that cannot realistically be concealed.

- Design a Common interpretation and a Mythic interpretation of the same idea.

- Decide whether the feature changes rarity by itself or only when combined with other major traits.

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
The best way to understand **Decorative Wings** is to imagine the character dealing with it on a boring Tuesday, not only during a transformation scene.

The useful questions here are **load paths, range of motion, proprioception, attachment or suspension logic, and the way nearby structures make room for it**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **Decorative Wings**, practical details can include doorway and ceiling clearance, folding geometry while sitting, keeping the wings from blocking people in crowded spaces, and air load during fast movement. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **Decorative Wings** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include one wing locking into a safer folded state, loss of fine feather or membrane control, and asymmetric lift or drag. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **Decorative Wings** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include nanites reinforcing the leading edge, support seams becoming visible near the shoulder roots, and a deliberate half-fold used as a resting posture. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through air load during fast movement, doorway and ceiling clearance, and harness and clothing design—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **Decorative Wings**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. The safest fallback is usually a mechanically conservative posture or reduced range, not the anatomy vanishing for no reason. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- What does **Decorative Wings** feel like when nothing is wrong?
- What is the first small sign that **Decorative Wings** is overloaded, damaged, or badly calibrated?
- Does **Decorative Wings** behave differently during a Glassshift, active repair, or emotional stress?
- Which parts of **Decorative Wings** are automatic, and which can be deliberately controlled?

#### Character-facing note

**Decorative Wings** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.

This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Additional Eyes**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Additional Eyes** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, additional eyes matters through doors, chairs, beds, vehicles, hugs, carrying objects, sports, workspaces, and learning where every new body part is without staring at it. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note stance, gait, reach, turning radius, resting position, clothing cuts, furniture fit, and how the form looks when actually moving instead of posing. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of additional eyes so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Decide whether the feature is congenital, constructed, acquired, or the result of a later Glassshift.

- Describe how the feature changes clothing, furniture, movement, or sleeping posture.

- Give the feature a visual tell that becomes obvious during a Glassshift.

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
The short version is useful, but **Additional Eyes** becomes a lot easier to write once it is treated as part of somebody’s ordinary life.

The useful questions here are **load paths, range of motion, proprioception, attachment or suspension logic, and the way nearby structures make room for it**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **Additional Eyes**, practical details can include field-of-view overlap, deciding which eyes track a speaker, reading displays at different focal distances, and sleep masks or protective eyewear. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **Additional Eyes** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include one optic switching to low-resolution mode, a display eye freezing while biological vision remains usable, and double images. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **Additional Eyes** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include pupils or display shapes narrowing under load, nanite cleaning patterns crossing the lens, and one optic dimming to reduce processing. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through deciding which eyes track a speaker, glare and brightness control, and reading displays at different focal distances—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **Additional Eyes**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. The safest fallback is usually a mechanically conservative posture or reduced range, not the anatomy vanishing for no reason. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- What is the first small sign that **Additional Eyes** is overloaded, damaged, or badly calibrated?
- Which parts of **Additional Eyes** are automatic, and which can be deliberately controlled?
- How does **Additional Eyes** affect clothing, furniture, sleep, travel, or personal space?
- What would a Noxivitre medic see about **Additional Eyes** that an ordinary observer would miss?

#### Character-facing note

**Additional Eyes** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.

Horns and Antlers is a morphology option rather than a mandatory species trait. It should still look BlackGlass-built: the joints, attachment points, floating gaps, plating, and mutation seams should make the feature feel native to the species instead of pasted on.

- Account for whether the trait can be voluntarily suppressed.

In-world, **Horns and Antlers** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: sleeping posture, protecting the horn base from repeated impacts, headwear, and doorframes and low ceilings can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **Horns and Antlers**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

A useful way to understand horns and antlers is to separate what the character sees from what BlackGlass and the nanites are actually doing underneath. It connects to body geometry, socket placement, balance, collision clearance, coordination, and BlackGlass-supported structural variation. The working substrate is the body map, skeletal or synthetic anchors, nerves, actuators, nanite bridges, and adaptive tissue around the changed body plan. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands horns and antlers, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for horns and antlers is a cool-looking design that has no room to move, duplicated structures that collide with each other, poor center of mass, or too many systems competing for the same space. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. If a character breaks the normal version of **Liquid-Nanite Limbs**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. Local function can survive degraded network contact, but precision and repair speed usually drop before basic survival does. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- What does **Liquid-Nanite Limbs** feel like when nothing is wrong?
- Which parts of **Liquid-Nanite Limbs** are automatic, and which can be deliberately controlled?
- Does **Liquid-Nanite Limbs** behave differently during a Glassshift, active repair, or emotional stress?
- What is the first small sign that **Liquid-Nanite Limbs** is overloaded, damaged, or badly calibrated?

#### Character-facing note

**Liquid-Nanite Limbs** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.


**PART V — MORPHOLOGY & TRAIT CATALOG • ENTRY 119 · [ATLAS](#nox_atlas) / [PART INDEX](#part-v-quick-index)**
