# **Digitigrade Builds**

Digitigrade Builds is a morphology option rather than a mandatory species trait. It should still look BlackGlass-built: the joints, attachment points, floating gaps, plating, and mutation seams should make the feature feel native to the species instead of pasted on.

- Design around whether the trait can be voluntarily suppressed.

- Decide what happens when the trait is damaged.

- Account for what social assumptions are attached to it.

- A character can hide a trait without erasing it from their body map. Concealment is presentation, not nonexistence.

- Unobtanium should remain special through lore and permission, not by banning ordinary creators from having fun anatomy.

In practice, this can show up through details like layered cybernetic joints, ear or horn structures that integrate with the skull rather than looking glued on, or moving surface patterns that react to emotion. None of those are mandatory; they are examples of how the same rule can produce different silhouettes while still reading as part of one species.

In-world, **Digitigrade Builds** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: sleep, clothing, ordinary social interaction, and privacy can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **Digitigrade Builds**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

A useful way to understand digitigrade builds is to separate what the character sees from what BlackGlass and the nanites are actually doing underneath. It connects to body geometry, socket placement, balance, collision clearance, coordination, and BlackGlass-supported structural variation. The working substrate is the body map, skeletal or synthetic anchors, nerves, actuators, nanite bridges, and adaptive tissue around the changed body plan. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands digitigrade builds, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for digitigrade builds is a cool-looking design that has no room to move, duplicated structures that collide with each other, poor center of mass, or too many systems competing for the same space. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for digitigrade builds before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Digitigrade Builds** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Digitigrade Builds** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as a more compact resting state and subtle BlackGlass seams should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For digitigrade builds, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Digitigrade Builds**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Digitigrade Builds** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, digitigrade builds matters through doors, chairs, beds, vehicles, hugs, carrying objects, sports, workspaces, and learning where every new body part is without staring at it. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note stance, gait, reach, turning radius, resting position, clothing cuts, furniture fit, and how the form looks when actually moving instead of posing. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of digitigrade builds so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Decide what the nanites do when the feature is damaged.

- Design a Common interpretation and a Mythic interpretation of the same idea.

- Describe how the feature changes clothing, furniture, movement, or sleeping posture.

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
For **Digitigrade Builds**, the species rules should answer the practical questions first and leave spectacle for when the story actually needs it.

The useful questions here are **load paths, range of motion, proprioception, attachment or suspension logic, and the way nearby structures make room for it**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **Digitigrade Builds**, practical details can include maintenance, sleep, privacy, and ordinary social interaction. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through clothing, sleep, and movement—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

The safest fallback is usually a mechanically conservative posture or reduced range, not the anatomy vanishing for no reason. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for aquatic builds before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Aquatic Builds** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Aquatic Builds** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as visible nanite traffic under load and a more compact resting state should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For aquatic builds, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Aquatic Builds**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Aquatic Builds** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, aquatic builds matters through doors, chairs, beds, vehicles, hugs, carrying objects, sports, workspaces, and learning where every new body part is without staring at it. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note stance, gait, reach, turning radius, resting position, clothing cuts, furniture fit, and how the form looks when actually moving instead of posing. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of aquatic builds so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Decide whether the feature is congenital, constructed, acquired, or the result of a later Glassshift.

- Describe how the feature changes clothing, furniture, movement, or sleeping posture.

- Define what a medical scanner would call this feature.

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
The short version is useful, but **Aquatic Builds** becomes a lot easier to write once it is treated as part of somebody’s ordinary life.

The useful questions here are **load paths, range of motion, proprioception, attachment or suspension logic, and the way nearby structures make room for it**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **Aquatic Builds**, practical details can include clothing, privacy, ordinary social interaction, and sleep. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **Aquatic Builds** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include temporary fallback behavior, reduced precision, and extra heat or energy use. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **Aquatic Builds** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include subtle BlackGlass seams, visible nanite traffic under load, and a more compact resting state. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through clothing, ordinary social interaction, and sleep—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **Aquatic Builds**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. The safest fallback is usually a mechanically conservative posture or reduced range, not the anatomy vanishing for no reason. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- What is the first small sign that **Aquatic Builds** is overloaded, damaged, or badly calibrated?
- What misconception about **Aquatic Builds** would the character be tired of correcting?
- Does **Aquatic Builds** behave differently during a Glassshift, active repair, or emotional stress?
- Which parts of **Aquatic Builds** are automatic, and which can be deliberately controlled?

#### Character-facing note

**Aquatic Builds** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
**Morphology Summary and Combination Rules** is one of those details that can look simple on a reference sheet and turn into a dozen small decisions the moment the character starts moving.

The useful questions here are **load paths, range of motion, proprioception, attachment or suspension logic, and the way nearby structures make room for it**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **Morphology Summary and Combination Rules**, practical details can include ordinary social interaction, maintenance, clothing, and privacy. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **Morphology Summary and Combination Rules** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include extra heat or energy use, reduced precision, and temporary fallback behavior. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **Morphology Summary and Combination Rules** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include subtle BlackGlass seams, a more compact resting state, and visible nanite traffic under load. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through sleep, maintenance, and clothing—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **Morphology Summary and Combination Rules**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. The safest fallback is usually a mechanically conservative posture or reduced range, not the anatomy vanishing for no reason. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- What does **Morphology Summary and Combination Rules** feel like when nothing is wrong?
- Which parts of **Morphology Summary and Combination Rules** are automatic, and which can be deliberately controlled?
- What is the first small sign that **Morphology Summary and Combination Rules** is overloaded, damaged, or badly calibrated?
- What would a Noxivitre medic see about **Morphology Summary and Combination Rules** that an ordinary observer would miss?

#### Character-facing note

**Morphology Summary and Combination Rules** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.

# **Why Rarity Exists**

Why Rarity Exists is part of the rarity framework. Rarity measures how structurally unusual and BlackGlass-intensive a design is; it does not automatically decide strength, morality, status, intelligence, or how important the character is.

- Design around whether the trait can be voluntarily suppressed.

- Decide what happens when the trait is damaged.

- Account for what maintenance the nanites perform.

- If a trait is copied from another species concept, change its construction and reason for existing so it fits BlackGlass biology.

- Mutations should still obey the individual's body map unless the story explicitly establishes corruption or instability.

In practice, this can show up through details like moving surface patterns that react to emotion, visible core-light through translucent BlackGlass, or ear or horn structures that integrate with the skull rather than looking glued on. None of those are mandatory; they are examples of how the same rule can produce different silhouettes while still reading as part of one species.

In-world, **Why Rarity Exists** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: privacy, clothing, maintenance, and movement can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **Why Rarity Exists**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

In canon, why rarity exists sits inside the same body-map logic as every other Noxivitre feature. It connects to classification by structural complexity, BlackGlass intensity, and how far the body plan departs from the ordinary range. The working substrate is observable anatomy, stable mutation behavior, core architecture, documented Glassshift capacity, and the combination of major traits rather than one flashy detail. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands why rarity exists, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for why rarity exists is treating rarity as a power score, social rank, moral value, or excuse to lock ordinary anatomy behind permissions. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for why rarity exists before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Why Rarity Exists** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Why Rarity Exists** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as subtle BlackGlass seams and visible nanite traffic under load should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For why rarity exists, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Why Rarity Exists**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Why Rarity Exists** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, why rarity exists matters through how people talk about rarity, whether they care about it at all, how records classify someone, and how to prevent a label from replacing the character’s actual personality. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note how a design is labeled consistently while still leaving room for exceptions, mixed traits, reclassification, and personal style. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception. Riven Solace and Blade are the canon reference point for why rarity exists because they are Generation Zero: the first two Noxivitres. Riven entered that transition from an Uncommon Protogen baseline with concealed floating legs and tail, horns, and two ear pairs, while Blade entered from a much more ordinary Common Protogen baseline. Their different starting bodies make the pair unusually useful for separating inherited anatomy from genuinely Noxivitre-specific BlackGlass changes. When later lore is uncertain, the founders can be used as precedent without requiring every later Noxivitre to copy them.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of why rarity exists so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Give the feature a visual tell that becomes obvious during a Glassshift.

- Decide whether the feature is congenital, constructed, acquired, or the result of a later Glassshift.

- Define what a medical scanner would call this feature.

If a character breaks the normal version of **Common Overview**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. A classification disagreement should be solved by examining system complexity, not by arguing over which design looks more impressive. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- What would a Noxivitre medic see about **Common Overview** that an ordinary observer would miss?
- What is the first small sign that **Common Overview** is overloaded, damaged, or badly calibrated?
- Does **Common Overview** behave differently during a Glassshift, active repair, or emotional stress?
- How does **Common Overview** affect clothing, furniture, sleep, travel, or personal space?

#### Character-facing note

**Common Overview** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.

# **Common Trait Range**

Common Trait Range is part of the rarity framework. Rarity measures how structurally unusual and BlackGlass-intensive a design is; it does not automatically decide strength, morality, status, intelligence, or how important the character is.

- Baseline or lightly mutated body plan

- Usually two arms and two legs

- Minor floating segments are fine

- Simple horns, tails, ears, armor, or face variants

- BlackGlass remains highly stable

For Common designs, the visual target is consistency before spectacle. A character can still be simple or complicated inside the tier; the rarity name mainly tells other creators how far the anatomy has moved from the stable baseline and how much BlackGlass is actively involved in maintaining it.

A Common character can still share traits with neighboring tiers. Reclassification should happen when the whole design crosses a structural threshold, not because one tiny accessory, color choice, or cosmetic feature got added. This keeps the ladder useful instead of turning it into a checklist where every horn costs one rarity point.

This is the normal version of **Common Trait Range**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

In canon, common trait range sits inside the same body-map logic as every other Noxivitre feature. It connects to classification by structural complexity, BlackGlass intensity, and how far the body plan departs from the ordinary range. The working substrate is observable anatomy, stable mutation behavior, core architecture, documented Glassshift capacity, and the combination of major traits rather than one flashy detail. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands common trait range, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for common trait range is treating rarity as a power score, social rank, moral value, or excuse to lock ordinary anatomy behind permissions. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for common trait range before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Common Trait Range** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Common Trait Range** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as a more compact resting state and subtle BlackGlass seams should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For common trait range, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Common Trait Range**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Common Trait Range** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, common trait range matters through how people talk about rarity, whether they care about it at all, how records classify someone, and how to prevent a label from replacing the character’s actual personality. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note how a design is labeled consistently while still leaving room for exceptions, mixed traits, reclassification, and personal style. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of common trait range so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Decide whether the feature is congenital, constructed, acquired, or the result of a later Glassshift.

- Define what a medical scanner would call this feature.

- Describe how the feature changes clothing, furniture, movement, or sleeping posture.

Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Uncommon Trait Range** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, uncommon trait range matters through how people talk about rarity, whether they care about it at all, how records classify someone, and how to prevent a label from replacing the character’s actual personality. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note how a design is labeled consistently while still leaving room for exceptions, mixed traits, reclassification, and personal style. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of uncommon trait range so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Decide whether the feature is congenital, constructed, acquired, or the result of a later Glassshift.

- Describe how the feature changes clothing, furniture, movement, or sleeping posture.

- Give the trait one practical downside that is not just 'it hurts.'

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
**Uncommon Trait Range** is one of those details that can look simple on a reference sheet and turn into a dozen small decisions the moment the character starts moving.

The useful questions here are **whole-body complexity, dependency count, active BlackGlass load, stability, and whether the concept changes canon authority rather than merely appearance**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **Uncommon Trait Range**, practical details can include maintenance, movement, privacy, and sleep. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **Uncommon Trait Range** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include slower response, reduced precision, and temporary fallback behavior. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **Uncommon Trait Range** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include visible nanite traffic under load, a more compact resting state, and subtle BlackGlass seams. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through clothing, sleep, and ordinary social interaction—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **Uncommon Trait Range**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. A classification disagreement should be solved by examining system complexity, not by arguing over which design looks more impressive. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- What does **Uncommon Trait Range** feel like when nothing is wrong?
- What misconception about **Uncommon Trait Range** would the character be tired of correcting?
- What is the first small sign that **Uncommon Trait Range** is overloaded, damaged, or badly calibrated?
- Which parts of **Uncommon Trait Range** are automatic, and which can be deliberately controlled?

#### Character-facing note

**Uncommon Trait Range** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.

# **Uncommon Example Builds**

Uncommon Example Builds is part of the rarity framework. Rarity measures how structurally unusual and BlackGlass-intensive a design is; it does not automatically decide strength, morality, status, intelligence, or how important the character is.

- Noticeably altered body plan

- Four arms or several floating parts are normal examples

- Multiple ears, larger horns, split tails, or moderate adaptive structures

- More visible BlackGlass behavior

- Still easy to stabilize

For Uncommon designs, the visual target is consistency before spectacle. A character can still be simple or complicated inside the tier; the rarity name mainly tells other creators how far the anatomy has moved from the stable baseline and how much BlackGlass is actively involved in maintaining it.

A Uncommon character can still share traits with neighboring tiers. Reclassification should happen when the whole design crosses a structural threshold, not because one tiny accessory, color choice, or cosmetic feature got added. This keeps the ladder useful instead of turning it into a checklist where every horn costs one rarity point.

This is the normal version of **Uncommon Example Builds**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

The important thing about uncommon example builds is that it has to work inside a mutable Noxivitre body, not only look good in a reference sheet. It connects to classification by structural complexity, BlackGlass intensity, and how far the body plan departs from the ordinary range. The working substrate is observable anatomy, stable mutation behavior, core architecture, documented Glassshift capacity, and the combination of major traits rather than one flashy detail. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands uncommon example builds, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for uncommon example builds is treating rarity as a power score, social rank, moral value, or excuse to lock ordinary anatomy behind permissions. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for uncommon example builds before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Uncommon Example Builds** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Uncommon Example Builds** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as subtle BlackGlass seams and a more compact resting state should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For uncommon example builds, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

This is the normal version of **Rare Example Builds**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

For Noxivitres, rare example builds is treated as a real system rather than a decorative trait. It connects to classification by structural complexity, BlackGlass intensity, and how far the body plan departs from the ordinary range. The working substrate is observable anatomy, stable mutation behavior, core architecture, documented Glassshift capacity, and the combination of major traits rather than one flashy detail. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands rare example builds, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for rare example builds is treating rarity as a power score, social rank, moral value, or excuse to lock ordinary anatomy behind permissions. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for rare example builds before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Rare Example Builds** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Rare Example Builds** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as subtle BlackGlass seams and visible nanite traffic under load should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For rare example builds, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Rare Example Builds**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Rare Example Builds** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, rare example builds matters through how people talk about rarity, whether they care about it at all, how records classify someone, and how to prevent a label from replacing the character’s actual personality. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note how a design is labeled consistently while still leaving room for exceptions, mixed traits, reclassification, and personal style. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of rare example builds so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Describe how the feature changes clothing, furniture, movement, or sleeping posture.

- Decide whether the feature changes rarity by itself or only when combined with other major traits.

- Write a version that is subtle enough to hide and another that cannot realistically be concealed.

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
A good version of **Rare Example Builds** feels specific to the person wearing it. The system can be technically complicated without making the character talk like a manual.

The useful questions here are **whole-body complexity, dependency count, active BlackGlass load, stability, and whether the concept changes canon authority rather than merely appearance**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **Rare Example Builds**, practical details can include ordinary social interaction, clothing, movement, and maintenance. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **Rare Example Builds** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include slower response, reduced precision, and temporary fallback behavior. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **Rare Example Builds** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include subtle BlackGlass seams, a more compact resting state, and visible nanite traffic under load. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through privacy, clothing, and movement—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **Rare Example Builds**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. A classification disagreement should be solved by examining system complexity, not by arguing over which design looks more impressive. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- What misconception about **Rare Example Builds** would the character be tired of correcting?
- What does **Rare Example Builds** feel like when nothing is wrong?
- What would a Noxivitre medic see about **Rare Example Builds** that an ordinary observer would miss?
- How does **Rare Example Builds** affect clothing, furniture, sleep, travel, or personal space?

#### Character-facing note

**Rare Example Builds** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.

The short version is useful, but **Legendary Example Builds** becomes a lot easier to write once it is treated as part of somebody’s ordinary life.

The useful questions here are **whole-body complexity, dependency count, active BlackGlass load, stability, and whether the concept changes canon authority rather than merely appearance**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **Legendary Example Builds**, practical details can include stairs and uneven ground, seat height, stride timing, and how the pelvis compensates during fast turns. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **Legendary Example Builds** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include shortened stride, temporary balance assistance from a tail or nanite field, and one leg reverting to a conservative gait. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **Legendary Example Builds** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include stance widening under load, bridge effects becoming visible near a floating leg, and actuator seams tightening during a climb. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through seat height, stairs and uneven ground, and stride timing—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **Legendary Example Builds**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. A classification disagreement should be solved by examining system complexity, not by arguing over which design looks more impressive. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- How does **Legendary Example Builds** affect clothing, furniture, sleep, travel, or personal space?
- What would a Noxivitre medic see about **Legendary Example Builds** that an ordinary observer would miss?
- What does **Legendary Example Builds** feel like when nothing is wrong?
- What misconception about **Legendary Example Builds** would the character be tired of correcting?

#### Character-facing note

**Legendary Example Builds** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.


**PART VI — RARITY SYSTEM • ENTRY 140 · [ATLAS](#nox_atlas) / [PART INDEX](#part-vi-quick-index)**

# **Mythic Overview**

Mythic is the highest fully open Noxivitre rarity and fills the same broad design niche that rare/restricted variants often fill in other cyber-organic species: this is where the huge, bizarre, anatomy-breaking concepts are expected to live. Mythic is still open to everyone; it is intentionally the tier that prevents cool extreme traits from being shoved into the creator-locked category just because they look impressive.

- Highest open rarity

- Reserved for the wildest stable designs, not for permission gating

- Massive mutation complexity, unusual core behavior, extreme floating anatomy, or multiple forms

- Can look almost impossible while remaining internally consistent

- No creator permission required

For Mythic designs, the visual target is consistency before spectacle. A character can still be simple or complicated inside the tier; the rarity name mainly tells other creators how far the anatomy has moved from the stable baseline and how much BlackGlass is actively involved in maintaining it.

A Mythic character can still share traits with neighboring tiers. Reclassification should happen when the whole design crosses a structural threshold, not because one tiny accessory, color choice, or cosmetic feature got added. This keeps the ladder useful instead of turning it into a checklist where every horn costs one rarity point.

This is the normal version of **Mythic Overview**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

The important thing about mythic overview is that it has to work inside a mutable Noxivitre body, not only look good in a reference sheet. It connects to classification by structural complexity, BlackGlass intensity, and how far the body plan departs from the ordinary range. The working substrate is observable anatomy, stable mutation behavior, core architecture, documented Glassshift capacity, and the combination of major traits rather than one flashy detail. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands mythic overview, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for mythic overview is treating rarity as a power score, social rank, moral value, or excuse to lock ordinary anatomy behind permissions. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for mythic overview before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Mythic Overview** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Mythic Overview** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as subtle BlackGlass seams and a more compact resting state should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For mythic overview, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Mythic Overview**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Mythic Overview** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, mythic overview matters through how people talk about rarity, whether they care about it at all, how records classify someone, and how to prevent a label from replacing the character’s actual personality. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note how a design is labeled consistently while still leaving room for exceptions, mixed traits, reclassification, and personal style. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception. Founder status and rarity remain separate concepts, but Riven and Blade are confirmed Unobtanium Noxivitres. Their individual traits do not automatically become Unobtanium-only just because the founders have them: six arms, floating anatomy, huge mutations, Fracturefaces, multiple ears, horns, and complicated BlackGlass behavior can all exist in open tiers when the overall design fits. What is locked is the founder-class core architecture and creator-approved canon authority carried by their Origin Glasshearts. A future Mythic character can be visually more extreme than either founder without breaking the system. This distinction keeps Unobtanium meaningful without turning the rarity ladder into a design paywall.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of mythic overview so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Decide whether the feature changes rarity by itself or only when combined with other major traits.

- Design a Common interpretation and a Mythic interpretation of the same idea.

- Give the feature a visual tell that becomes obvious during a Glassshift.

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
The short version is useful, but **Mythic Overview** becomes a lot easier to write once it is treated as part of somebody’s ordinary life.

The useful questions here are **whole-body complexity, dependency count, active BlackGlass load, stability, and whether the concept changes canon authority rather than merely appearance**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **Mythic Overview**, practical details can include sleep, ordinary social interaction, movement, and privacy. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Useful warning signs for this feature include slower response, reduced precision, and temporary fallback behavior. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **Mythic Overview** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include visible nanite traffic under load, subtle BlackGlass seams, and a more compact resting state. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through ordinary social interaction, maintenance, and clothing—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **Mythic Overview**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. A classification disagreement should be solved by examining system complexity, not by arguing over which design looks more impressive. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- How does **Mythic Overview** affect clothing, furniture, sleep, travel, or personal space?
- What does **Mythic Overview** feel like when nothing is wrong?
- Does **Mythic Overview** behave differently during a Glassshift, active repair, or emotional stress?

Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. ### **DEEPER CANON**

A useful way to understand mythic example builds is to separate what the character sees from what BlackGlass and the nanites are actually doing underneath. It connects to classification by structural complexity, BlackGlass intensity, and how far the body plan departs from the ordinary range. The working substrate is observable anatomy, stable mutation behavior, core architecture, documented Glassshift capacity, and the combination of major traits rather than one flashy detail. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands mythic example builds, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for mythic example builds is treating rarity as a power score, social rank, moral value, or excuse to lock ordinary anatomy behind permissions. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for mythic example builds before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Mythic Example Builds** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Mythic Example Builds** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as visible nanite traffic under load and a more compact resting state should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
**Unobtanium Trait Range** is one of those details that can look simple on a reference sheet and turn into a dozen small decisions the moment the character starts moving.

That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **Unobtanium Trait Range**, practical details can include movement, sleep, clothing, and ordinary social interaction.
