That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands step four: pick a rarity, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for step four: pick a rarity is treating rarity as a power score, social rank, moral value, or excuse to lock ordinary anatomy behind permissions. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for step four: pick a rarity before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Step Four: Pick a Rarity** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Step Four: Pick a Rarity** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as subtle BlackGlass seams and a more compact resting state should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For step four: pick a rarity, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Step Four: Pick a Rarity**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Step Four: Pick a Rarity** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, step four: pick a rarity matters through how people talk about rarity, whether they care about it at all, how records classify someone, and how to prevent a label from replacing the character’s actual personality. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note how a design is labeled consistently while still leaving room for exceptions, mixed traits, reclassification, and personal style. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of step four: pick a rarity so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Give the trait one practical downside that is not just 'it hurts.'

- Decide whether the feature is congenital, constructed, acquired, or the result of a later Glassshift.

- Design a Common interpretation and a Mythic interpretation of the same idea.

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
The short version is useful, but **Step Four: Pick a Rarity** becomes a lot easier to write once it is treated as part of somebody’s ordinary life.

The useful questions here are **whole-body complexity, dependency count, active BlackGlass load, stability, and whether the concept changes canon authority rather than merely appearance**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **Step Four: Pick a Rarity**, practical details can include sleep, privacy, movement, and maintenance. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **Step Four: Pick a Rarity** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include slower response, extra heat or energy use, and temporary fallback behavior. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **Step Four: Pick a Rarity** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include subtle BlackGlass seams, visible nanite traffic under load, and a more compact resting state. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through ordinary social interaction, movement, and clothing—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **Step Four: Pick a Rarity**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. A classification disagreement should be solved by examining system complexity, not by arguing over which design looks more impressive. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- Does **Step Four: Pick a Rarity** behave differently during a Glassshift, active repair, or emotional stress?
- What misconception about **Step Four: Pick a Rarity** would the character be tired of correcting?
- What is the first small sign that **Step Four: Pick a Rarity** is overloaded, damaged, or badly calibrated?
- What would a Noxivitre medic see about **Step Four: Pick a Rarity** that an ordinary observer would miss?

#### Character-facing note

**Step Four: Pick a Rarity** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.

**Step Seven: Decide What Is Hidden** is one of those details that can look simple on a reference sheet and turn into a dozen small decisions the moment the character starts moving.

The useful questions here are **accessibility, fashion, privacy, regional custom, economics, architecture, and the fact that no single community represents every Noxivitre**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **Step Seven: Decide What Is Hidden**, practical details can include maintenance, clothing, movement, and privacy. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **Step Seven: Decide What Is Hidden** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include slower response, reduced precision, and temporary fallback behavior. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **Step Seven: Decide What Is Hidden** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include visible nanite traffic under load, subtle BlackGlass seams, and a more compact resting state. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through privacy, clothing, and sleep—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **Step Seven: Decide What Is Hidden**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. Social friction is not biological failure. Communities can solve the same practical problem in different ways. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- What misconception about **Step Seven: Decide What Is Hidden** would the character be tired of correcting?
- Which parts of **Step Seven: Decide What Is Hidden** are automatic, and which can be deliberately controlled?
- What does **Step Seven: Decide What Is Hidden** feel like when nothing is wrong?
- How does **Step Seven: Decide What Is Hidden** affect clothing, furniture, sleep, travel, or personal space?

#### Character-facing note

**Step Seven: Decide What Is Hidden** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.

# **Step Eight: Decide Mutation History**

Step Eight: Decide Mutation History is a creator-facing rule meant to make character design easier. The goal is to give enough structure that characters read as the same species while leaving enough freedom that two creators can make radically different designs.

- Check how another species might misunderstand it.

- Check what the trait looks like when the individual is exhausted.

- Check how the individual learned to coordinate it.

- Use at least one species-specific visual such as clean silhouettes even when the anatomy is complex.

- Make sure the result still has an actual personality and life outside the body design.

Use this page as a build tool rather than lore that every character has to recite. If a choice does not matter for the character, skip it; if a choice creates a better design question, follow it even if the answer is weird.

A finished character should be explainable in a few sentences even if their body is extremely complicated. Complexity is fine; confusion is not the goal. The BlackGlass logic should make the strange parts feel connected to each other.

This is the normal version of **Step Eight: Decide Mutation History**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

In canon, step eight: decide mutation history sits inside the same body-map logic as every other Noxivitre feature. It connects to mutation triggers, body-map rewriting, stabilization, and long-term mutation memory. The working substrate is active BlackGlass, dormant BlackGlass, Vitrite support swarms, core signaling, and the individual’s existing anatomy template. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands step eight: decide mutation history, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for step eight: decide mutation history is runaway rewriting, rejection, contradictory body maps, incomplete stabilization, or a Glassshift that keeps trying to solve a problem after the problem is gone. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for step eight: decide mutation history before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Step Eight: Decide Mutation History** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Step Eight: Decide Mutation History** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as subtle BlackGlass seams and visible nanite traffic under load should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For step eight: decide mutation history, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Step Eight: Decide Mutation History**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Step Eight: Decide Mutation History** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, step eight: decide mutation history matters through how someone plans around stress, repairs, medical scans, accidental triggers, body changes, and the possibility that yesterday’s anatomy is not exactly today’s. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note what changes first, what stays recognizable, how quickly the change stabilizes, and what evidence remains after the event. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception. Riven Solace and Blade are the canon reference point for step eight: decide mutation history because they are Generation Zero: the first two Noxivitres. Riven entered that transition from an Uncommon Protogen baseline with concealed floating legs and tail, horns, and two ear pairs, while Blade entered from a much more ordinary Common Protogen baseline. Their different starting bodies make the pair unusually useful for separating inherited anatomy from genuinely Noxivitre-specific BlackGlass changes. When later lore is uncertain, the founders can be used as precedent without requiring every later Noxivitre to copy them.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of step eight: decide mutation history so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Write a version that is subtle enough to hide and another that cannot realistically be concealed.

- Decide what the nanites do when the feature is damaged.

- Design a Common interpretation and a Mythic interpretation of the same idea.

# **Common Character Checklist**

Common Character Checklist is a creator-facing rule meant to make character design easier. The goal is to give enough structure that characters read as the same species while leaving enough freedom that two creators can make radically different designs.

- Baseline or lightly mutated body plan

- Usually two arms and two legs

- Minor floating segments are fine

- Simple horns, tails, ears, armor, or face variants

- BlackGlass remains highly stable

For Common designs, the visual target is consistency before spectacle. A character can still be simple or complicated inside the tier; the rarity name mainly tells other creators how far the anatomy has moved from the stable baseline and how much BlackGlass is actively involved in maintaining it.

A Common character can still share traits with neighboring tiers. Reclassification should happen when the whole design crosses a structural threshold, not because one tiny accessory, color choice, or cosmetic feature got added. This keeps the ladder useful instead of turning it into a checklist where every horn costs one rarity point.

This is the normal version of **Common Character Checklist**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

In canon, common character checklist sits inside the same body-map logic as every other Noxivitre feature. It connects to classification by structural complexity, BlackGlass intensity, and how far the body plan departs from the ordinary range. The working substrate is observable anatomy, stable mutation behavior, core architecture, documented Glassshift capacity, and the combination of major traits rather than one flashy detail. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands common character checklist, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for common character checklist is treating rarity as a power score, social rank, moral value, or excuse to lock ordinary anatomy behind permissions. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for common character checklist before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Common Character Checklist** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Common Character Checklist** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as visible nanite traffic under load and a more compact resting state should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For common character checklist, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Common Character Checklist**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Common Character Checklist** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, common character checklist matters through how people talk about rarity, whether they care about it at all, how records classify someone, and how to prevent a label from replacing the character’s actual personality. A practical reference sheet can note how a design is labeled consistently while still leaving room for exceptions, mixed traits, reclassification, and personal style. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of common character checklist so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Give the feature a visual tell that becomes obvious during a Glassshift.

- Describe how the feature changes clothing, furniture, movement, or sleeping posture.

- Decide whether the feature changes rarity by itself or only when combined with other major traits.

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
For **Common Character Checklist**, the species rules should answer the practical questions first and leave spectacle for when the story actually needs it.

The useful questions here are **whole-body complexity, dependency count, active BlackGlass load, stability, and whether the concept changes canon authority rather than merely appearance**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **Common Character Checklist**, practical details can include sleep, movement, privacy, and ordinary social interaction. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **Common Character Checklist** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include reduced precision, extra heat or energy use, and slower response. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **Common Character Checklist** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include a more compact resting state, subtle BlackGlass seams, and visible nanite traffic under load. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through maintenance, clothing, and sleep—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **Common Character Checklist**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. A classification disagreement should be solved by examining system complexity, not by arguing over which design looks more impressive. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- Does **Common Character Checklist** behave differently during a Glassshift, active repair, or emotional stress?
- What would a Noxivitre medic see about **Common Character Checklist** that an ordinary observer would miss?
- What misconception about **Common Character Checklist** would the character be tired of correcting?
- How does **Common Character Checklist** affect clothing, furniture, sleep, travel, or personal space?

#### Character-facing note

**Common Character Checklist** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.

With **Legendary Character Checklist**, practical details can include stride timing, shoe or paw protection, stairs and uneven ground, and how the pelvis compensates during fast turns. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **Legendary Character Checklist** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include misjudged foot placement, temporary balance assistance from a tail or nanite field, and one leg reverting to a conservative gait. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **Legendary Character Checklist** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include stance widening under load, actuator seams tightening during a climb, and bridge effects becoming visible near a floating leg. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through shoe or paw protection, seat height, and stride timing—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **Legendary Character Checklist**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. A classification disagreement should be solved by examining system complexity, not by arguing over which design looks more impressive. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- What would a Noxivitre medic see about **Legendary Character Checklist** that an ordinary observer would miss?
- Which parts of **Legendary Character Checklist** are automatic, and which can be deliberately controlled?
- What does **Legendary Character Checklist** feel like when nothing is wrong?
- What misconception about **Legendary Character Checklist** would the character be tired of correcting?

#### Character-facing note

**Legendary Character Checklist** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.

# **Mythic Character Checklist**

Mythic Character Checklist is a creator-facing rule meant to make character design easier. The goal is to give enough structure that characters read as the same species while leaving enough freedom that two creators can make radically different designs.

- Highest open rarity

- Reserved for the wildest stable designs, not for permission gating

- Massive mutation complexity, unusual core behavior, extreme floating anatomy, or multiple forms

- Can look almost impossible while remaining internally consistent

- No creator permission required

For Mythic designs, the visual target is consistency before spectacle. A character can still be simple or complicated inside the tier; the rarity name mainly tells other creators how far the anatomy has moved from the stable baseline and how much BlackGlass is actively involved in maintaining it.

A Mythic character can still share traits with neighboring tiers. Reclassification should happen when the whole design crosses a structural threshold, not because one tiny accessory, color choice, or cosmetic feature got added. This keeps the ladder useful instead of turning it into a checklist where every horn costs one rarity point.

This is the normal version of **Mythic Character Checklist**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

In canon, mythic character checklist sits inside the same body-map logic as every other Noxivitre feature. It connects to classification by structural complexity, BlackGlass intensity, and how far the body plan departs from the ordinary range. The working substrate is observable anatomy, stable mutation behavior, core architecture, documented Glassshift capacity, and the combination of major traits rather than one flashy detail. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands mythic character checklist, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for mythic character checklist is treating rarity as a power score, social rank, moral value, or excuse to lock ordinary anatomy behind permissions. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for mythic character checklist before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Mythic Character Checklist** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Mythic Character Checklist** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as a more compact resting state and visible nanite traffic under load should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For mythic character checklist, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Mythic Character Checklist**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Mythic Character Checklist** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, mythic character checklist matters through how people talk about rarity, whether they care about it at all, how records classify someone, and how to prevent a label from replacing the character’s actual personality. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note how a design is labeled consistently while still leaving room for exceptions, mixed traits, reclassification, and personal style. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception. Founder status and rarity remain separate concepts, but Riven and Blade are confirmed Unobtanium Noxivitres. Their individual traits do not automatically become Unobtanium-only just because the founders have them: six arms, floating anatomy, huge mutations, Fracturefaces, multiple ears, horns, and complicated BlackGlass behavior can all exist in open tiers when the overall design fits. What is locked is the founder-class core architecture and creator-approved canon authority carried by their Origin Glasshearts. A future Mythic character can be visually more extreme than either founder without breaking the system. This distinction keeps Unobtanium meaningful without turning the rarity ladder into a design paywall.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of mythic character checklist so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Write a version that is subtle enough to hide and another that cannot realistically be concealed.

- Give the trait one practical downside that is not just 'it hurts.'

- Decide whether the feature changes rarity by itself or only when combined with other major traits.

- Account for what emotional states make it more noticeable.

- Damage and mutation are different states. A missing part is not automatically a new trait, and a new trait is not automatically an injury.

- BlackGlass can be weird without being random. Repeated motifs, copied anatomy, and consistent nanite behavior make extreme designs feel intentional.

In practice, this can show up through details like adaptive armor that changes with posture, temporary nanite scaffolding, or visible core-light through translucent BlackGlass. None of those are mandatory; they are examples of how the same rule can produce different silhouettes while still reading as part of one species.

In-world, **Trait Exceptions** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: sleep, maintenance, ordinary social interaction, and movement can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **Trait Exceptions**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

In canon, trait exceptions sits inside the same body-map logic as every other Noxivitre feature. It connects to character-design decisions, readability, rarity classification, personal history, and the minimum rules that make an OC feel like a Noxivitre. The working substrate is the chosen body base, BlackGlass pattern, Vitrite behavior, mutation history, limits, personality, and visual construction language. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands trait exceptions, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for trait exceptions is building a checklist instead of a person, copying a Protogen silhouette too closely, using rarity as a substitute for design, or stacking traits without deciding how any of them function together. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for trait exceptions before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Trait Exceptions** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Trait Exceptions** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as subtle BlackGlass seams and visible nanite traffic under load should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For trait exceptions, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **Trait Exceptions**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Trait Exceptions** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, trait exceptions matters through how the character moves, dresses, talks, maintains their body, reacts to mutation, interacts with others, and exists when nothing dramatic is happening. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note whether the design can be explained clearly, drawn consistently, written in motion, and recognized as the same character before and after a Glassshift. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of trait exceptions so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Write one example of the trait on a calm character and one on a stressed character.

- Give the trait one practical downside that is not just 'it hurts.'

- Decide whether the feature is congenital, constructed, acquired, or the result of a later Glassshift.

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
The best way to understand **Trait Exceptions** is to imagine the character dealing with it on a boring Tuesday, not only during a transformation scene.

The useful questions here are **accessibility, fashion, privacy, regional custom, economics, architecture, and the fact that no single community represents every Noxivitre**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **Trait Exceptions**, practical details can include sleep, clothing, movement, and privacy. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **Trait Exceptions** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include reduced precision, slower response, and temporary fallback behavior. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **Trait Exceptions** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include a more compact resting state, subtle BlackGlass seams, and visible nanite traffic under load. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through ordinary social interaction, clothing, and sleep—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **Trait Exceptions**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. Social friction is not biological failure. Communities can solve the same practical problem in different ways. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- Does **Trait Exceptions** behave differently during a Glassshift, active repair, or emotional stress?
- What would a Noxivitre medic see about **Trait Exceptions** that an ordinary observer would miss?
- What misconception about **Trait Exceptions** would the character be tired of correcting?
- What does **Trait Exceptions** feel like when nothing is wrong?

#### Character-facing note

**Trait Exceptions** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. That separation is important to the open-species side of the canon.

Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **Avoiding Protogen Copying** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, avoiding protogen copying matters through how the character moves, dresses, talks, maintains their body, reacts to mutation, interacts with others, and exists when nothing dramatic is happening. The most convincing Noxivitre designs show at least a few of those consequences even when nothing is going wrong. A practical reference sheet can note whether the design can be explained clearly, drawn consistently, written in motion, and recognized as the same character before and after a Glassshift. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception. Riven and Blade also make the species’ ancestry impossible to hide, which is useful rather than embarrassing. They began as Protogens, so Noxivitres are allowed to acknowledge Protogen influence directly; the important part is what happened next. BlackGlass stopped functioning like an accessory and became the system that rewrote their body maps, supported detached or duplicated structures, and created a new stable cyber-organic architecture. Noxivitre design should therefore look like an evolutionary or mutagenic divergence from that starting point, not like a Protogen with a new label pasted over it.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of avoiding protogen copying so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**

- Write one example of the trait on a calm character and one on a stressed character.

- Give the feature a visual tell that becomes obvious during a Glassshift.

- Describe how the feature changes clothing, furniture, movement, or sleeping posture.

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
The short version is useful, but **Avoiding Protogen Copying** becomes a lot easier to write once it is treated as part of somebody’s ordinary life.

The useful questions here are **accessibility, fashion, privacy, regional custom, economics, architecture, and the fact that no single community represents every Noxivitre**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **Avoiding Protogen Copying**, practical details can include maintenance, movement, privacy, and sleep. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **Avoiding Protogen Copying** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include temporary fallback behavior, slower response, and reduced precision. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **Avoiding Protogen Copying** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include subtle BlackGlass seams, a more compact resting state, and visible nanite traffic under load. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through movement, clothing, and privacy—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **Avoiding Protogen Copying**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. Social friction is not biological failure. Communities can solve the same practical problem in different ways. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- Does **Avoiding Protogen Copying** behave differently during a Glassshift, active repair, or emotional stress?
- What would a Noxivitre medic see about **Avoiding Protogen Copying** that an ordinary observer would miss?
- What does **Avoiding Protogen Copying** feel like when nothing is wrong?
- How does **Avoiding Protogen Copying** affect clothing, furniture, sleep, travel, or personal space?

**Avoiding Protogen Copying** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. # **Designing a Distinct Face**

Use fractured plates, exposed biological muzzle sections, floating display shards, split masks, asymmetrical digital surfaces, or other BlackGlass-driven structures. The point is to build a face system around this species' mutation logic instead of defaulting to the familiar rounded Protogen visor.

- Design around what social assumptions are attached to it.

- Decide how another species might misunderstand it.

- Account for whether the body can rebuild it from a stored template.

- Damage and mutation are different states. A missing part is not automatically a new trait, and a new trait is not automatically an injury.

- A character can hide a trait without erasing it from their body map. Concealment is presentation, not nonexistence.

In practice, this can show up through details like visible core-light through translucent BlackGlass, tails with visible mutation history, or moving surface patterns that react to emotion. None of those are mandatory; they are examples of how the same rule can produce different silhouettes while still reading as part of one species.

In-world, **Designing a Distinct Face** is not something the character has to explain every time it appears. It becomes background life: cleaning seams between plates, privacy around diagnostic displays, eating and drinking, and impact protection can all be affected without turning every scene into a biology lecture. The rule is here so those little consequences stay consistent when the story is busy talking about something else.

This is the normal version of **Designing a Distinct Face**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

For Noxivitres, designing a distinct face is treated as a real system rather than a decorative trait. It connects to character-design decisions, readability, rarity classification, personal history, and the minimum rules that make an OC feel like a Noxivitre. The working substrate is the chosen body base, BlackGlass pattern, Vitrite behavior, mutation history, limits, personality, and visual construction language. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands designing a distinct face, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for designing a distinct face is building a checklist instead of a person, copying a Protogen silhouette too closely, using rarity as a substitute for design, or stacking traits without deciding how any of them function together. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for designing a distinct face before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **Designing a Distinct Face** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **Designing a Distinct Face** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as plates separating slightly during strong emotion and internal light visible through seams should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

### Human Notes & Practical Detail
**Character-Creation Summary** is one of those details that can look simple on a reference sheet and turn into a dozen small decisions the moment the character starts moving.

The useful questions here are **accessibility, fashion, privacy, regional custom, economics, architecture, and the fact that no single community represents every Noxivitre**. That is the technical side, but it should show up in ordinary life instead of only in diagrams. With **Character-Creation Summary**, practical details can include clothing, movement, maintenance, and sleep. A character who has had the feature for years usually handles those things without thinking; somebody who acquired it recently may still misjudge space, overcorrect, or consciously plan movements that will eventually become automatic.

Decide what **Character-Creation Summary** feels like from the inside. It might register as ordinary proprioception, pressure, a quiet digital position sense, background diagnostics, or almost nothing until something goes wrong. Useful warning signs for this feature include reduced precision, slower response, and temporary fallback behavior. Those signs do not need to mean catastrophic failure. Noxivitre systems usually degrade in layers, so reduced precision or a safer fallback state often appears before anything truly dangerous happens.

For artists and writers, give **Character-Creation Summary** at least one repeatable visual or behavioral tell. Possibilities include visible nanite traffic under load, a more compact resting state, and subtle BlackGlass seams. Keep the tell consistent enough that it feels like the same body from scene to scene. Also test the feature somewhere inconvenient but mundane: a cramped vehicle, an unfamiliar bed, a clinic designed for fixed anatomy, or a crowded hallway. If the design still has a believable answer there—perhaps through ordinary social interaction, sleep, and clothing—the rule is doing real work instead of existing only for spectacle.

If a character breaks the normal version of **Character-Creation Summary**, write down what is compensating for the exception and what tradeoff appears somewhere else. Social friction is not biological failure. Communities can solve the same practical problem in different ways. Rarity should still be judged from the whole build. A visually extreme version can remain inside the open tiers, including Mythic, when it does not use creator-reserved founder authority. Unobtanium is not a reward for having the loudest silhouette.

#### Questions worth answering

- What misconception about **Character-Creation Summary** would the character be tired of correcting?
- Does **Character-Creation Summary** behave differently during a Glassshift, active repair, or emotional stress?
- What would a Noxivitre medic see about **Character-Creation Summary** that an ordinary observer would miss?

#### Character-facing note

**Character-Creation Summary** can shape habits, accessibility needs, confidence, embarrassment, fashion, or body language, but it should not replace the character's personality. Noxivitres can have extremely different bodies without those bodies deciding morality, intelligence, social importance, or fighting ability. # **BlackGlass Outbreak Scenario**

BlackGlass Outbreak Scenario is a seed rather than a fixed storyline. It exists so the setting can grow outward from the same BlackGlass rules without forcing every character into one canon plot.

- Immediate problem: how it changes balance and movement

- Character problem: how the individual learned to coordinate it

- BlackGlass complication: what the trait looks like when the individual is exhausted

- Escalation should change the body or the interpretation of the body, not just raise the danger level.

- The ending can resolve the event without resolving every mutation it caused.

A strong version of this scenario should make the species rules matter to the plot. Use details such as ear or horn structures that integrate with the skull rather than looking glued on, visible BlackGlass seams, or nonuniform crystalline surfaces as evidence of what BlackGlass is doing instead of explaining everything through exposition.

The scenario is deliberately open enough to be horror, drama, comedy, action, or slice-of-life depending on the cast. What makes it species-specific is that the body itself can become part of the consequence and remain changed after the immediate problem is over.

This is the normal version of **BlackGlass Outbreak Scenario**, not a ban on future exceptions. If a later character breaks the default, document what changed, what supports the exception, and whether the change is personal or actually updates species-wide canon.

### **DEEPER CANON**

The important thing about blackglass outbreak scenario is that it has to work inside a mutable Noxivitre body, not only look good in a reference sheet. It connects to mutation triggers, body-map rewriting, stabilization, and long-term mutation memory. The working substrate is active BlackGlass, dormant BlackGlass, Vitrite support swarms, core signaling, and the individual’s existing anatomy template. That means the feature should have a readable input, a physical or informational pathway, and a stable result; BlackGlass is flexible, but it is not an excuse for effects to happen with no internal reason. When a later writer expands blackglass outbreak scenario, the first question should be what part of the body map is being changed or interpreted, and the second should be what keeps that change stable after the dramatic moment is over.

The main failure state for blackglass outbreak scenario is runaway rewriting, rejection, contradictory body maps, incomplete stabilization, or a Glassshift that keeps trying to solve a problem after the problem is gone. Noxivitre biology usually tries to correct inconsistencies instead of immediately collapsing, so small errors can produce compensation: nanites reroute signals, BlackGlass reinforces weak structures, or the Glassheart temporarily limits a mutation until coordination catches up. That correction is not free. It can consume energy, create heat, reduce regeneration elsewhere, slow sensory processing, or force the individual to consciously manage something that would normally be automatic. These consequences are useful because they keep an extremely flexible species from becoming consequence-free while still allowing very strange bodies to function.

- Define the body-map entry for blackglass outbreak scenario before defining flashy secondary effects.

- Decide what keeps the feature stable while the individual is asleep, injured, distracted, or low on nanites.

### **BLACKGLASS & NANITE INTERACTION**

BlackGlass does not build **BlackGlass Outbreak Scenario** from a blank species template. It starts with the individual: their proportions, coloration, existing plating or fur, scars, learned movement, and the body map they already recognize as themselves. Vitrite swarms handle the fine integration work while the Glassheart checks whether the result still belongs to that person. That is why copied anatomy normally looks personal rather than generic. If **BlackGlass Outbreak Scenario** is duplicated or rebuilt, details such as a more compact resting state and visible nanite traffic under load should still fit the owner’s established design language unless corruption or deliberate experimentation is the point of the scene.

Control can be distributed instead of centralized. For blackglass outbreak scenario, the Glassheart sets the high-level body-map state, local BlackGlass handles structural adaptation, and nearby Vitrite swarms perform thousands of small corrections every second. If one layer is interrupted, the others may keep the feature functioning in a degraded state rather than switching it completely off. This gives writers room for partial failures: a floating segment may stay suspended but lose fine sensation, a display may keep working while expression becomes delayed, or a duplicated limb may remain healthy while coordination becomes clumsy. Partial failure is usually more interesting than treating every problem as either perfect function or total shutdown.

- Keep original coloration and personal construction language when BlackGlass duplicates an existing structure unless corruption is specifically part of the story.

- Give partial failures a readable symptom instead of making every malfunction an instant catastrophic shutdown.

### **RARITY, DAILY LIFE & EDGE CASES**

For **BlackGlass Outbreak Scenario**, rarity should be assigned by the whole build rather than by how flashy this one feature looks. Common is the stable/simple end of the scale; Uncommon adds noticeable complexity; Rare permits major structural deviation; Legendary stacks several demanding systems; Mythic is the intentionally extreme open tier. Unobtanium is different because it is creator-locked for founder-class or canon-authority reasons, not because it has the biggest number of limbs. A public character can therefore have an outrageous version of **BlackGlass Outbreak Scenario** and still remain Mythic if the concept does not require reserved founder mechanics.

In everyday life, blackglass outbreak scenario matters through how someone plans around stress, repairs, medical scans, accidental triggers, body changes, and the possibility that yesterday’s anatomy is not exactly today’s. None of this has to become constant exposition in a story; it is background logic that lets a character move naturally and lets artists or writers answer small questions consistently. Edge cases are allowed, but an exception should state what rule it breaks, why BlackGlass can support it, and what new limitation or tradeoff appears because of that exception. Riven Solace and Blade are the canon reference point for blackglass outbreak scenario because they are Generation Zero: the first two Noxivitres. Riven entered that transition from an Uncommon Protogen baseline with concealed floating legs and tail, horns, and two ear pairs, while Blade entered from a much more ordinary Common Protogen baseline. Their different starting bodies make the pair unusually useful for separating inherited anatomy from genuinely Noxivitre-specific BlackGlass changes. When later lore is uncertain, the founders can be used as precedent without requiring every later Noxivitre to copy them.

- Classify the entire design, not one isolated trait; rarity measures complexity and BlackGlass intensity, not worth or combat power.

- Write at least one mundane consequence of blackglass outbreak scenario so the feature still feels real outside transformation scenes.

### **EXPANSION HOOKS**
